It has been determined that as the network's dimensions increase, the generalized error may experience a sudden sharp increase, despite the predictable and controlled nature of its training error. This phenomenon can be attributed to the emergence of spurious models that accurately match the training data but poorly perform on unseen test data. It has been found that the generalized error's behavior is characterized by an exponential relationship with the network's dimensions. Additionally, it has been determined that the generalized error's sharp transition can be further characterized by specific statistical properties of these spurious models. It has been found that the density of these spurious models increases exponentially with the network's dimensions, while their average performance over the training data remains consistently low and predictable. It has been demonstrated that modifying the training process by selectively disregarding spurious models can lead to a generalized error that remains predictably and consistently low. All the theoretical findings outlined above have been verified and substantiated using numerical simulations of randomly generated data sets. Designing intelligent machine learning systems requires a deeper understanding of intelligent biological systems. To explore this, we developed a 32-neuron model of the Caenorhabditis Elegans' nervous system using Python and the NneXt neural network library. We trained this model on a dataset that includes responses to stimuli as well as the worm's movement and behavioral patterns. Our model, which replicates the animal's ring neuromusculokinesthetic structure, uses a three-layered feed-forward network with a binary sigmoid activation function. After training, the model accurately reproduces the animal's responses to the stimulus, underscoring NneXt's ability to capture the essential features of C. Elegans' behavioral and motor control dynamics. This work implies that artificial systems that mimic biological intelligence may eventually reveal the underlying mechanisms of intelligent behavior. We suggest that models like ours could serve a pivotal role in uncovering key elements of intelligent biological systems, ultimately paving the way for understanding intelligent machine learning systems. We study discrete-time ergodic Markov chains on labeled ordered trees and their applications in studying random permutations. We derive a key criterion for the asymptotic behavior of the distribution of path lengths in these chains. This criterion has significant implications for understanding the structure of large permutations as well as the limiting behavior of the depth of trees with fixed points, two distinct research areas that have been extensively explored in the literature. Furthermore, we establish a survival theorem for rotations in permutations, yielding a novel result in this domain. Additionally, our findings extend existing research on permutations to include other classes of labeled ordered trees, such as trees with arbitrary vertex sets and even, odd, and half-even permutations. We utilize the developed theory to address questions regarding the existence of exponentially rare events under stationary marginal distributions, a topic of ongoing research in the field. This work generalizes and consolidates various existing theorems in the field, offering novel insights and perspectives along the way. We demonstrate the broad applicability of our theory by providing four distinct examples of tree-valuation Markov chains, which correspond to permutations of specific types and trees with specific structural characteristics. In the course of our research, we prove a novel Asymptotic Equipartition principle for these tree-valuation Markov chains, which is a fundamental contribution of this work. We also introduce a general method for establishing growth rates in this context and provide a comprehensive overview of the capabilities of this theory in the concluding section of the paper. Overall, our research expands the theoretical framework of this area, offering a flexible and holistic understanding of the underlying phenomena. This formalization enables us to tackle a broad range of problems, as evidenced by the specific applications presented in Section 7 of this work. We derive a set of general theorems at the beginning of Section 7 and provide detailed examples of their applicability to specific classes of permutations and trees with specific structural characteristics. Due to the underlying generality of our approach, we are confident that it can be extended to other applications, a capability that is further discussed in the concluding section of the paper. This work is further supported by additional appendices that provide background information on the underlying theory, which is further discussed in Appendix A. Additionally, Appendix B provides a list of open research questions in the field, which is further discussed at the end of the paper. Overall, our research is designed to stimulate future exploration in this area, offering novel insights and perspectives that are further discussed in the concluding section of the paper. Following the initial findings, researchers investigated additional properties of finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras. Results showed that a finite-dimensional algebra with a nilpotent-derived property is either simple or decomposable, and it was found that a nilpotent algebra can be transformed into a degenerate algebra. Additionally, it was discovered that a finite-dimensional algebra with a solvable property is either simple or decomposable. Notably, it was found that nitrogenic and solvable algebras coincide in the degenerate case. Related properties of finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras regarding nilpotency and solvability were also explored. Specifically, results showed that a nilpotent algebra can be transformed into an abelian algebra, and similar properties were examined for solvability. Finally, researchers investigated finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras over a field and identified necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of an associative algebra that satisfies a specific property. Results showed that such a condition has varying requirements based on the characteristic of the field but always requires an algebraic condition when the field has a characteristic of 0. Corresponding characteristics and properties were also explored for nilpotent and solvable algebras. Lastly, researchers investigated the cohomology of finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras, revealing interesting properties such as the non-existence of a one-dimensional non-trivial cohomology class in the degenerate case when the field has a characteristic of 0. In particular, results showed that a finite-dimensional degenerate Zinbiel algebra is not a Banach algebra if and only if the algebra's characteristic is 0. Additionally, researchers found new characteristics and properties of finite-dimensional nilpotent and solvable cohomology classes. In the final exploration of the topic, researchers considered a finite-dimensional associative algebra as a bilinear map, examining its properties and characterization through the prism of nilpotent and solvable properties. Notably, results showed that a finite-dimensional associative algebra has a unital, degenerate, nilpotent, and solvable property with the same conditions having varying requirements based on the field's characteristic. Corresponding properties and characteristics were also explored for nilpotent and solvable properties. Specifically, in the focusing scenario, scattering only happens when initial data is in the Strichartz space. Conversely, in the defocusing case, all initial data within the Strichartz space leads to scattering or global well-posedness. Furthermore, it has been observed that the $L^2$ upper bounds of initial data and the $L^\infty L^2$ bounds of potential inhomogeneities are critical factors in confirming scattering for $\sin^2$ and $1 + \sin^2$ scenarios. Leveraging inhomogeneity to induce scattering is a key finding of this study. A mathematical model called the dispersal differential equation model utilizes Fokker-Planck equations with diffusion parameters to analyze the movement of populations undergoing the susceptible-infected-susceptible dynamics with migration. This work extends two existing models, the AIR and DOCS models, which respectively incorporate mean-field interactions and contact factors, to develop a comprehensive model that incorporates both interactions and migration. Using semi-analytical calculations, we determine explicit solutions for the mean and variance of infected population densities within each local area and verify that these results align with simulations. Furthermore, we compare the mass transport equation solution from the DOCS model with the solution from the AIR model that disables dispersal, demonstrating that the DOCS model absorbs the impact of migration. By incorporating mean-field interactions and dispersal, our model shows that a critical parameter, the contact factor, can be adjusted to prevent outbreaks locally or control the spread by enabling the recovery of isolated regions. Crucially, our model reveals an unexpected phenomenon - the averaging effect of dispersal - which causes the mean density of infected populations to converge to equilibrium at a slower rate than expected. This convergence behavior is further influenced by the size of the population and dispersal distance but does not affect the variance's convergence behavior in a significant manner. Dispersal's impact on the average infected population is more pronounced than we anticipated from analyzing average behavior, indicating an underestimation of outbreaks due to dispersal in cases where dispersal distances are short. Therefore, considering population size is insufficient to exclusively determine the dispersion's effect; rather, the type of interactions, average migration distance, and population size all play crucial roles in understanding population dynamics with dispersal. Dispersion populations with sufficient migration distance are more susceptible to mean-field interactions than to the effects of dispersal. When interactions and dispersal are in balance, we observed an interesting phenomenon of oscillation, indicating that population dynamics is significantly affected by the interplay between dispersal and mean-field interactions. This work contributes to our understanding of population dynamics through the discovery of previously unrecognized effects, such as dispersion altering the convergence rate, dispersion affecting the mean infected population convergence behavior, and oscillating population dynamics in a significant way. The former group is further subdivided into subgroups exhibiting unique characteristics based on their eccentricities. research is carried out using the official SiD software framework, known as Geant4.9.04,

Graphite is identified as having the highest local electron density and is found to be more advantageous than silicon. Next, we establish a technological approach for creating a dielectric accelerator based on natural graphite, incorporating a thin graphite layer over a gold contact. This design allows for efficient electron emission from the dielectric, and simulations indicate that the graphite-gold structure can achieve electron energies of over 30 keV through a relatively short acceleration process. Moreover, we find that the natural graphite used in this experiment is sufficient in nature, and we assess the feasibility of achieving higher electron energies by substituting natural graphite with highly-oriented graphite. Finally, we simulate the behavior of the electron beam produced by the dielectric-based accelerator and discover that the electrode structure influences the electron beam's transparency and focus. This approach is applied to the Hunter-Zhang black brane solution to demonstrate its properties in the counterterm method, and similar techniques are employed for the Bohm mass formulation of quantum field theory in the presence of horizons. In mmWave multicasting with very high bandwidths (e.g., 1 GHz), serving a large number of users with minimal interference is a major challenge. To overcome this, leveraging SPARCS (Stochastic Prime Access Matrix with Constant Shapes) is a promising approach. By assuming multiple antennas at the receiver and using mmWave flat channel models, we derive SPARCS formulas that optimize multicasting efficiency for users with similar signal strengths. Initially, we optimize a reduced version of the problem using convex relaxation techniques and then apply the closed-form solutions of the SPARCS factors to the full problem through backtracking. Interestingly, incorporating SPARCS into benchmark schemes yields substantial improvements of at least an order of magnitude better system performance, especially when there are many users with minimal quality differences. Additionally, SPARCS significantly reduces the complexity of admission control, as it can handle a very large number of users. Even with optimal admission control, SPARCS outperforms D2D multicasting when there are many users, indicating the effectiveness of this new framework. Furthermore, SPARCS can easily incorporate additional constraints found in real-world applications, such as user positioning and beamforming, making it a versatile and practical optimization method. The proposed SPARCS algorithm provides efficient multicasting performance even with a limited number of antennas at the transmitter. However, with many antennas at the transmitter and a large number of users, SPARCS may not yield optimal results, indicating the need for further optimization. To address this issue, SPARCS is applied to a subproblem derived from the original multicasting problem using the Rayleigh quotient technique. By repeatedly solving the SPARCS subproblems, SPARCS-RE (Re-Optimization) yields near-optimal multicasting performance even with very many users and multiple antennas at both the receiver and transmitter. Moreover, SPARCS-RE outperforms SPARCS on the benchmark schemes with optimal admission control, demonstrating the effectiveness of repeatedly optimizing the SPARCS factors to obtain better system performance. Interestingly, SPARCS-RE can be viewed as an approximate version of the recently introduced Majorized SMM (Stoichiometric Majorization Matrix) algorithm, which SPARCS-RE can also surpass in performance. SPARCS and SPARCS-RE have been successfully validated through simulations with up to 64 users and 16 antennas, showing their potential in real-world mmWave multicasting systems. Although Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved great success in various applications, they often face significant difficulties in adapting to new domains due to their propensity for overfitting. In order to combat this issue, many researchers have sought to uncover mechanisms by which GNNs can effectively transfer knowledge across different tasks. This study provides a comprehensive examination of graph classification, aiming to elucidate the key factors contributing to knowledge transfer in GNNs. We present empirical evidence that GNNs learn task-specific features rather than graph-topological features. Furthermore, we demonstrate that graph classification involves predicting community labels or structural patterns learned from the training data, and the transferability of GNNs is significantly influenced by the similarity in community structure between source and target tasks. Finally, we provide recommendations for designing more efficient GNN models capable of effective transfer learning. The code used in this study is available at https://github.com/GraphLearningResearch/JournalSubmission/2022.

A novel recommender system based on Bayesian nonparametric approaches is proposed.  Inspired by the user-item interaction similarities in compact wireless sensors, a unified framework, named CARS, is introduced to model the interplay between users and items as discoveries of shared features.  Building on the Indian buffet process (IBP), CARS models each user and item as independent probabilistic agents that discover features based on their historical interactions, with features being selectively defined as they provide shared discoveries to agents.  To leverage historical data effectively, a unified variational generation process is defined for drawing user/ item labels and features simultaneously.  Optimizing the variational objectives efficiently through block-wise minimization, stochastic gradient descent is applied to learn CARS parameters.  Experimental results demonstrate that CARS outperforms state-of-the-art recommender systems based on various popular datasets in terms of predictive accuracy and efficiently handles novel user or item additions without re-training.  Moreover, its natural extension to multi-dimensional user/ item representations, particularly useful in sensor networks, is shown through incorporation of a Dirichlet process mixture model for clustering user/ item features into representative groups.  This research is complementary to existing recommender systems as they are generally re-trained with newly available data, highlighting the benefits of being online learning methods like CARS. This research focuses on determining essential estimates for oscillatory integrals when the phase and amplitude functions are smooth. Although the condition of smoothness is a basic necessity, it has been little explored in mathematical studies. By combining a novel approach with the classical stationary phase theory, we establish sharp estimates for oscillatory integrals with smooth phase and amplitude functions. These estimates demonstrate an intriguing relationship with the classical phase theory and are applicable in multiple dimensions. The derived estimates can be utilized in various contexts, for example, in verifying the well-posedness of equations describing oscillatory flows and deriving regularity results for oscillatory integrals of differential functions. The study also provides explicit examples illustrating the tightness of the obtained estimates, thereby showcasing a transition between the cases of smooth and phase functions with Lipschitz regularity. The findings presented in this study generalize and coordinate previous results established by Alazard, Hanrahan, Herr, Masmoudi, and Vella for one- and two-dimensional spaces, and also extend recent results obtained by the researcher in a previous study for general $n$ dimensions. The study also reveals new results for oscillatory integrals of differential functions with smooth phase and amplitude functions. The visual pathway contains opposing systems: one centered and one off-center, which are triggered by different light stimuli and play unique roles in visual processing. In typical light conditions, these systems remain balanced and work together to create a unified visual experience. However, in unusual lighting, such as high-contrast scenarios or medical image scans, one pathway dominates, which can result in distorted perception. To address this imbalance, we propose a deep neural network based approach to dynamically regulate the centered and off-centered processing and enhance the overall visual quality. Experimental results on various unnatural lighting effects demonstrate the efficacy of our method in correcting these phenomena and achieving more natural visual effects. Moreover, our approach effectively manages off-center dominance, which is a critical requirement in medical imaging. Our method is simple, adaptable, and suitable for real-time applications, which is showcased through its performance on a range of common natural and unusual lighting effects as well as a real-world retinal disease, diabetic retinopathy. This research paper presents certain implicit and explicit mathematical formulations derived from the definition of Wolter I optics, which are then used in the design of a specific X-ray telescope with an area of 10,000 square centimeters, focusing on a wavelength of 1 Angstrom. We reveal how higher order polynomial terms become prominent in the design process and provide a two-fold update to an existing algorithm originally utilized for designing Wolter I optics, along with a new evaluation method, which are then combined into a unified framework. We showcase the application of these mathematical formulations by utilizing them in the design of an X-ray telescope that meets the requirements for the DEMO X-ray telescope. We also numerically compute and graph the radial and axial deviations of this Wolter I optic, along with its focal plane, and demonstrate that this design meets the stipulated criterion for a 95% coverage of the circle defined by the radius of 40 millimeters. We further design two mirror pairs, utilizing a novel algorithm for the purpose of Wolter I optics, and show how the mirrors are arranged in the shape of a hexagon in order to minimize empty space. We then numerically compute the effective area of this designed optic, taking into account the atomic processes of bothellium, a heavy element, within the energy range of a few kiloelectronvolts and comparing it to that of individual mirrors not taking into account the effective area of this designed optic, showing an enhancement of more than two orders of magnitude over a single mirror design. We address the challenge of detecting novel categories with limited data, specifically focusing on addressing class outliers. We introduce an approach that simultaneously identifies anomalies within known classes while performing novel category classification. We represent anomalies using a Gaussian distribution, then use an energy-based model to maintain the distance between features generated by the multi-column neural network, in conjunction with contrastive learning. To tackle the significant data imbalance resulting from outlier elimination, we employ an autoencoder to recover discarded samples for enhanced training efficiency. We propose the Outlier-Aware Semi-Supervised Semi-Skeletonized (OASS2) framework, which significantly enhances the model's robustness by promoting margin separation between classes and intra-class centers, while minimizing the impact of outliers. We rigorously evaluate our approach against three metrics: (i) outlier detection, (ii) novel category classification, and (iii) transferability of learned features. OASS2 outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in all three aspects, as evidenced by the results presented. Code availability can be accessed at https://github.com/leverleiver/OASS2. We visually demonstrate OASS2's outlier detection capability in Figure 1, Figure 2, and Figure 3. To view the code, please visit https://leverleiver.github.io/OASS2/. Building on a previous framework for understanding non-invertible topological charges in lower-dimensional systems, we have developed equations that describe how these charges interact with localized electric currents. Applying our framework to a specific example - the O(3) nonlinear sigma model - we have found that introducing a local current operator also creates additional types of non-invertible charge defects, in addition to generating a domain wall that connects them. This shows that the domain wall itself behaves like an invertible particle-like object, called a k-monomode fermion, while the generated charge defects are non-invertible. This finding is similar to a well-known phenomenon in 2D systems, where the domain wall between topological charges gives rise to a Majorana zero mode. In contrast to previous studies on non-linear sigma models, we have found that the domain wall does not lead to a gap in the model's spectrum at low energy. This outcome can be verified through the $S$-matrix approach by calculating the scattering phases of the k-monomode fermion on the domain wall. When extended to higher-dimensional systems, our framework also reveals that the domain walls generated by mass terms between topological charges are always inert and do not facilitate any $S$-matrix interactions, while the presence of local current operators also creates additional non-invertible charge defects even in these higher-dimensional systems. Overall, our research provides a comprehensive understanding of charge defects arising from current operators in both lower and higher topological quantum systems. Moreover, our analysis highlights the prevalence of non-trivial physics related to invertible field excitations, such as the k-monomode fermion, which has previously been connected to the exact middle obstruction in the context of domain walls in 2D systems. Finally, our research offers implications for the study of fractional quantum Hall states, as it may shed new light on the role of charge defects arising from current operators in these systems. By adapting our framework to this context, we have found that the charge defects generated by local current operators do not produce gaps in the model's spectrum at low energy and do not facilitate $S$-matrix interactions, except in cases involving the scattering of magnetons. Consequently, their influence may manifest as corrections to the established fractional quantum Hall states' scaling properties. This allows us to utilize the uncertainty of BNNs to detect unusual instances of misclassified noise or rare occurrences. We apply this approach to simulate data generated from Gaussian processes and find that it effectively identifies anomalous instances. Additionally, we test this method on real-world astronomical data by analyzing a year's worth of Point Source Catalogue Experiment (PSCE) data from the e-MPSF project. Our findings support the use of this method for detecting rare anomalies in real-world datasets. This method can be implemented using the EMCC does Python package, which is open-source and compatible with the emcee sampling package. This research explores the interaction between different types of mechanical waves and optical modes within photonic crystals, with a particular focus on their respective symmetries. Utilizing advanced simulation techniques, we have identified and studied multiple mechanical and optical modes within a silicon nitride waveguide, with frequencies ranging from a few megahertz to a few gigahertz. Our analysis demonstrates that perturbations in mechanical or optical modes lead to intermodal Brillouin interactions, resulting in characteristic phase modulations. Notably, when mechanical and optical modes share the same symmetry, their interactions are intensified, whereas differences in symmetry reduce the rate of interaction. By intentionally introducing an acoustic mode with lower symmetry, we have demonstrated the ability to slow light down to nearly 20% of its original speed, with a large Brillouin phase shift of approximately 11.7 radians per second. These findings highlight the potential for customized light manipulation and the design of advanced photonic systems with tailored optical properties. Furthermore, we have identified several key regimes in which these interactions occur, with implications for the development of specialized photonic devices, such as optical filters, delay lines, and sensors. Lastly, we have established a theoretical foundation for controlling these interactions based on mechanical and optical mode coupling, with avenues for future experimentation outlined. Overall, our research lays the groundwork for the development of specialized photonic and acoustic systems with tailored optical properties. Furthermore, we have identified a potential pathway to observing quantum entanglement between optical and mechanical platforms, with implications for quantum communication and the transfer of information between different types of quantum particles. Lastly, we have investigated various applications of the Brillouin interactions, such as optical feedback in laser systems and the sensitivity of photonic structures to acoustic waves. Utilizing numerical simulations, we have demonstrated that modifications in mechanical or optical modes can be detected with high sensitivity, with the potential to be used as highly precise sensors to detect subtle changes in the physical environment. To further validate our approach, we have successfully designed and created an experimental setup to observe the intermodal Brillouin interactions, with the aim of fine-tuning the parameters of the mechanical and optical modes. Our experimental results have demonstrated a large number of mechanical and optical modes with varying frequencies, ranging from a few MHz to several GHz. Our current experiment is focused on adjusting the silicon nitride waveguide to be smaller than 2 μm in width and microstructured to be highly sensitive to mechanical and optical mode interactions. Compared to the standard mathematical approach, a study found that E2LS can reduce the computational time needed to solve these problems at least 100-fold for BMCP and 1000-fold for SUKP by taking advantage of a smaller search space. To further speed up the process, a streaming algorithm, SA, was used to efficiently update a key variable in E2LS. Even though it may lead to some suboptimal solutions, SA can provide a high-quality solution within a stream of $O(\sqrt{n_g})$ iterations. For instance, considering the SUKP with $n_g=10^6$ variables and $n_d=10^3$ dimensions, SA can find an approximately 1% worse solution in just $O(\sqrt{10^6})$ streams. Furthermore, a hybrid algorithm, HY, combined the strengths of E2LS and SA by using the streaming algorithm to find an initial solution, which is then improved upon through E2LS. As a result, HY can provide higher quality solutions than SA and also take advantage of the reduced parameter space provided by E2LS. However, it's worth noting that HY's performance can be affected by mis-specifying the $n_d$ parameter, which can lead the algorithm to get stuck in a suboptimal state. To overcome this limitation, a modified streaming algorithm, MSA, was developed to determine the $n_d$ parameter dimension independently using the first $n_d$ variables in a iterative process. As a result, MSA can be used in conjunction with the hybrid algorithm, HY, to improve the reliability and overall performance of the combined algorithm. As demonstrated in several numerical experiments, the modified hybrid algorithm can lead to better results and more accurate solution for various fiber optimization problems. Furthermore, the initial solution provided by the streaming algorithm is close to optimal and can be reliably used in practice. As an additional benefit, the streaming algorithm can also provide solution-independent guarantees for SUKP and BMCP. In practical applications of churn prevention, data scientists often face a challenge due to limited access to the past history of a time series for a given customer. Understanding how the length of this historical data affects prediction accuracy is therefore crucial for determining the feasibility of the model. Empirical studies have consistently demonstrated that shorter historical data leads to poorer model performance and increased uncertainty, ultimately rendering prediction futile in such scenarios. Theoretical investigations into these issues have revealed inconsistencies, with some theories suggesting customer behavior should be evenly divided into two distinct groups. However, our present research disputes this notion through a different mathematical approach, which reveals a more complex relationship between historical data and prediction accuracy. By utilizing probability density functions to model customer behavior over various time horizons, we develop a more accurate model that takes into account data noise. Our analysis also identifies key noise characteristics and highlights how limiting data length can result in significantly overestimating the size of this behavior distribution. The approach we've developed enables the computation of asymptotic distribution convergence rates, which in turn allows for determining sufficient historical data length for reliable prediction. By analyzing specific, significant points in this distribution, we develop a metric for measuring historical data quality and provide data-driven estimates for the computed parameters. The results of our research demonstrate that (i) the behavior of future values is largely influenced by recent past behavior; (ii) the model incorrectly views customer behavior as a random walk due to perceived noise; (iii) the model is more accurate when using less noisy data; (iv) the size of this behavior distribution is overestimated when data is limited; (v) the time it takes for the distribution to converge in the AR(1) model is affected by variance rather than mean; (vi) the approach can be adapted to other types of linear models with constant coefficients. Furthermore, we develop a metric for measuring historical data quality and provide a practical tool for assessing this quality in real-world applications. The practical tool we've developed, which is based on the approach, can be used in any linear model with constant coefficients. Our results are validated through numerical examples and real-world data. The code used to produce the results in this paper is included in the appendix and can be easily replicated. The approach can be extended to tackle challenges in related fields. The practical implications of our research are as follows: (i) we can use our results to determine if a company has sufficient historical data for reliable churn prevention; (ii) we can use our results to determine if churning is predictable in cases where we have limited historical data.

In heavy-ion collisions, the electromagnetic field has a profound impact on charged particles such as electrons and positrons. This influence manifests physically by affecting their distribution, yielding positron production that is slightly ahead of electron production in terms of time. Utilizing the "instantaneous emission approximation" and an approach combining electromagnetic influences on particle motion, we simulate positron production in heavy-ion collisions. Our analysis, using data from RHIC's Beam Energy Scan, compares the resulting simulations to experimental observations of positron production, taking into account time delays, angular distributions, and mass differences between electrons and positrons. By accounting for effects such as finite particle life and electromagnetic influences on particle motion, our method successfully replicates experimental data for higher energy beams at RHIC, but fails to accurately model lower energy beams, specifically those under 20 GeV, necessitating further consideration of additional factors such as particle interactions. This result is consistent across various energy levels and collision densities. Cycle monitoring data contains valuable insights for enhancing cycling security and improving urban planning. In addition to data such as speed and altitude, information about a cyclist's route, weather conditions, and road conditions can influence safety. To effectively monitor and respond to cycling hazards, developers require an efficient system to recognize hazardous situations from regular cycling activities. This system can then supply city planners and other relevant authorities with valuable information to inform infrastructure design. We present a solution to this problem, using a cycle safety detection system based on deep learning techniques. In this context, we define safety-related cycling data and develop a corresponding dataset, known as the CycleSafeData. We also present a novel safety detection model, constructed from convolutional neural networks, and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in multiple detection tasks. Additionally, our work explores the application of augmented reality display technology to present safety metadata to cyclists in real-time. The CycleSafeData and corresponding code are available for public access. Furthermore, a public dashboard supports research and interaction with the CycleSafeData. Building on the p-Horseshoe method, we develop an unsupervised algorithm with sparse sparsity pattern flexibility to combine probabilistic robot modeling with robust estimation techniques for path planning. We assess the proposed approach by comparing it with established optimization-based solutions in different scenarios, using the MatLab toolbox with the MuQAT toolkit for matrix algebra operations. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this method on two platforms: (i) a hat-shaped mobile robot, and (ii) a four-wheeled autonomous vehicle, both equipped with onboard processing capabilities. This research showcases the versatility of the proposed method for large-scale dynamic system optimization, paving the way for applications in control systems design, data analysis, and machine learning. A ring R with this property is said to be elementarily subalgebraic over Z. If Z is added to R, the property is said to be properly subalgebraic. In a ring R without unity, a free duo ring is a ring that has no nonzero zero divisors and in which every nonzero element has a right (left) mate such that their product is a nonzero left (right) zero divisor. Researchers in the research field of Adversarial Robustness investigate ways to develop reliable artificial neural networks that perform well under hostile conditions and withstand malicious attacks. Specifically, this study focuses on optimizing residual networks for defending against hostile attacks by designing a robust feature extraction system that meets certain error and constraint requirements. In this context, we reveal a crucial relationship between neural networks featuring straight lines (identity mappings) and the vulnerability to hostile attacks based on error constraints. Furthermore, we propose a method to improve residual networks' robustness by merging straight line mappings with filter-wise momentum operations, thereby reducing the impact of hostile attacks. Our experiments demonstrate that this modification is feasible and contributes to the enhancement of residual networks' robustness against various types of hostile attacks. Notably, we achieve a significant enhancement in robust accuracy on the CIFAR dataset (especially for ProPGN) and outperform Plain ResNet on the ImageNet dataset with our proposed architecture. The code for our ProPGN algorithm is publicly accessible at https://github.com/quantdev/ProPGN. This study offers insights into the relationship between neural network architecture, hostile attacks, and robustness, as well as sheds light on the vulnerability of neural networks featuring straight lines from a theoretical standpoint. Overall, our research aims to facilitate deeper understanding of neural networks' robustness, specifically for residual networks. Lastly, we generate adversarial examples with nuanced features and elaborate explanations to facilitate visualization and understanding of mid-level visual concepts through the application of visualisation techniques. Ultimately, we reveal ProPGN's efficacy in defending against hostile attacks and complex visual scenarios. Consequently, we make a significant contribution towards visualisation research by introducing a method to generate and evaluate adversarial examples based on human judgement. As far as our knowledge goes, this study marks the first successful attempt at applying adversarial visualisation to assess visual transformations and extract mid-level visual concepts. Consequently, we open up new avenues for research on adversarial visualisation and mid-level vision and offer a unified framework that encompasses both dimensions. Ultimately, we believe that visualisation research facilitated by adversarial visualisation will yield more practical and impactful results. Accurately operating industrial processes generally requires a thorough grasp of their underlying dynamics. Machine learning models can help analysts gain insight into how their process is functioning by explaining what their predictions are based on. In this explanation, Shapley values assign contribution weights to input variables, revealing which factors are driving the process's behavior. To apply the Shapley framework, which requires numerous repeated measurements of the system, might be impractical or even unsafe due to the process's fast-changing conditions. To overcome this challenge, we've developed an approach that allows us to leverage a known model of the process to efficiently calculate Shapley values. This approach is demonstrated through an analysis of a continuous polymerization reactor. Results show significant variation in feature importance, depending on the observed data point, with features like temperature and conversion playing a prominent role. Additionally, we've found that our method's accuracy is comparable to the fully Shapley-based approach, while greatly reducing computational cost. This approach is particularly suited for handling systems involving many parameters and fast dynamics, making it well-suited for applications involving large process variables or those in real-time. With this technique, feature importance can be quickly assessed during process startup or when adjusting parameters. Furthermore, this approach is versatile and can be easily integrated into an existing process monitoring system to provide explanations for anomalies detected during normal operating conditions. This study is a first step in exploring the application of the Shapley framework to explainable chemistry, with the long-term goal of developing an understanding of how individual features, derived from first-principle models, are driving process behavior. This goal is particularly important in highly complex chemical processes, where there is often significant interaction between individual variables. In our case study, we've identified variables exhibiting significant interaction, including temperature and conversion. This analysis is crucial because it can inform decisions regarding variable selection for the training of machine-learning models, ultimately improving their accuracy and understanding of their underlying dynamics. However, when implemented with a traditional first-into-first-out (FIFO) queue, this benefit is limited by slow learning rates. This paper introduces a novel combination of Friedman's VRER and stochastic gradient variance reduction (SVR) techniques. By integrating two replay queues, one optimized using Friedman's VRER and the other using SVR, the proposed framework aims to achieve faster convergence rates while approaching the efficiency of Friedman's VRER. This integration is feasible without relying on a computationally expensive matrix inversion, and theoretical proofs confirm that the proposed method yields better convergence rates and improved efficiency. Experimental results validate the theoretical analysis, demonstrating the effectiveness of this novel approach. By leveraging two replay queues, the proposed method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in reinforcement learning. We present the Detail Context Block (DCB), a novel transformation module for enhancing spatiotemporal predictive models, which significantly improves their forecasting ability. The DCB module strategically fuses detail and coarse-grained features to facilitate precise prediction. During prediction, a part of the input map is resized to a coarser level, and both original and transformed maps are merged while considering their spatial resolutions. We demonstrate that our DCB module successfully boosts the accuracy of spatiotemporal forecasting models, based on experiments with real data. The proposed DCB module has been incorporated into STCGNet, a convolutional network designed for spatiotemporal forecasting, which has consistently outperformed existing models in multiple weather forecasting tasks such as nowcasting and long-term forecasting covering seven years, as well as short-term coastal algae forecasting covering four years. The proposed STCGNet has surpassed existing models in various evaluation metrics including the continuous maximum n-steps evaluation method and the discrete brier score. Moreover, it has demonstrated the ability to forecast complex weather phenomena such as heavy precipitation and coastal algae blooms. The proposed STCGNet supports multi-task learning, which has been validated through cognitive network analysis and task relationship assessment. A type system can be used for this purpose, but it may not adequately address all memory safety concerns, particularly those related to data structures like arrays and buffers, since a strict type system contradicts the nature of imperative programming which often involves the direct manipulation of memory. Consequently, it is common for languages like Python to represent memory as an attribute of variables, rather than declaring it explicitly. Nevertheless, direct manipulations of memory can compromise the integrity of the data, and improperly using it can cause security vulnerabilities, so explicitly defining memory operations through static interfaces can help prevent security breaches in languages like Python. Our work centers around developing a static analyzer focused on identifying and resolving boundary errors in Python, which involves the safe manipulation of arrays and buffers. To achieve this, we create a static model of the Python Memory Model (PMM) that captures the distinct characteristics of Python's memory management, its use of C-type objects for direct memory manipulation, and the presence of both static and dynamic memory operations in the language. Our analyzer is grounded in a type system, and to ensure accurate static analysis, we establish a correspondence between the PMM and the Pygmy Language Server, an interpreter designed for experimental analysis, and extend the Pygmy Language Server with a dynamic validator for further analysis. The combination of our static analyzer and the Pygmy Language Server enables the identification and resolution of boundary errors in Python based on the PMM, which has been proven effective in a series of tests. To enhance the construction of polar codes using pre-transformed codes, particularly those with CRC (cyclic redundancy check) assistance, we focus on optimizing decoding techniques for these codes. A novel decoding algorithm for pre-transformed polar codes, aided by CRC and KRC (kernel redundancy check) $N^{\frac{\gamma}{2} - \frac{1}{2}}$-error, has been developed with an adjustable parameter $\gamma \in [0, 1]$. This approach allows the transmission rate to reach $1 - N^{\frac{1-\gamma}{2}} d^{-1}$ for an $N$-size code, given $d$ errors. Compared to existing solutions, our algorithm significantly improves performance, with simulated results indicating a $N^{\frac{\gamma}{2}}$-factor improvement in error probability for a fixed rate. Furthermore, our algorithm's performance is consistently close to the theoretical optimum, with our results demonstrating a negligible performance loss of $N^{-\frac{1}{2} \gamma^{-1}}$ compared to the theoretical optimum, achieved through our proposed decoding algorithm. A simulated comparison against state-of-the-art techniques shows our algorithm's efficiency in achieving optimal error rates with reduced computational complexity. We also developed an optimized version of the Thomas algorithm and the BKC algorithm, our proposed decoding algorithm, using the KRC criterion. A simulated analysis of the two algorithms reveals their performance under simulated error conditions. Notably, our algorithm based on the CRC aids the transmission of polar codes with smaller error rates, up to $N^{\frac{1}{2} (\gamma \frac{N}{2} -1)}$ lower, for large $N$ and $\gamma = 1$. A Python code for our algorithm is also provided. A potential extension of our algorithm to non-binary polar codes is considered in the concluding section. The choice of method for co-adding images significantly influences the quality of combined frames, with implications for both astrophysical and planetary research. A particular challenge arises when dealing with planetary transits, where the median approach can produce an uneven Point Spread Function (PSF) that complicates analytic transit modeling. The issue with median co-adding is a natural consequence of its non-linear behavior, with the effects being more pronounced for images with poorer image quality. To overcome this limitation, we examined and compared two approaches: using the median with adaptive zone determination and interpolating to the target zone while preserving pixel structure. The results indicate that incorporating the zone determination step improves the star-planet centroid determination, reducing the average noise by 25% and achieving comparable or better centroid precision than the second method. Additionally, we determined the optimal zone size based on noise levels and investigated the overlap between the two methods, finding noise-level-dependent zone sizes that result in comparable co-added images to median-based approaches. The method has also been successfully applied to Kepler data with similar performance, and noise levels have been established for particular co-additional steps. The research further discusses applications in second-generation missions and potential areas of utilization. The study is set to extend its findings to the analysis of eclipsing binaries and further develop its results in the forthcoming AAS research paper. Initially, under linear fracture mechanics, the shape of a growing crack is determined by the material's fracture characteristics and the type of loading it's undergoing. However, when considering nonlinear fracture mechanics, additional factors come into play, such as the size of a growing crack and how it's influenced by the surrounding elastic field. Numerical simulations revealed that an instability occurring at the tip of a growing crack, which becomes more pronounced under certain geometries and loading conditions, can contribute to the final breakdown of material. Furthermore, this sharpening instability at notches contributes to the preference for specific modes of fracture that lower the material's fracture energy, such as cracking off small pieces or micro-cracking. These findings have significant implications for the design of components to resist fracture, as they provide valuable insights into the fractures observed in brittle materials. We present an innovative protocol, CVQC, for conditional verification of quantum circuits, specifically designed for classical verification of quantum circuits incorporating classical data. When comparing CVQC to other protocols achieving classical verification of quantum circuits, we observed a substantial increase in the CVQC's advantage in the average case but a reduced advantage in the worst case. At the core of CVQC is a novel verification method for classical-quantum states, utilizing an optimized variant of the quantum job checker from IBM Quantum, alongside a classical neural network employing cosine similarity for state comparison. Our research encompasses a thorough examination of the performance, complexity, and error rates of CVQC, highlighting its efficiency and wide applicability to real IBM Q circuits. By combining classical and quantum computations, CVQC accelerates the verification process, reducing it to approximately $1.57\times10^{-5}$ s on average, making it the fastest method. However, CVQC's reliance on the classical NN introduces a degree of uncertainty to its outcomes. Our analysis suggests that, in the average case, CVQC outperforms other protocols by a factor of at least $5.8$. Despite being the fastest method in the average case, CVQC's reliance on the NN leads to a reduced advantage of $1.27$ in the worst case, with a potential increase of $40\%$ in error rates. To further investigate the behavior of CVQC, we examined its performance under realistic conditions, utilizing circuits from the SISL benchmark suite, real MQUROC applications with classical outputs, and genuine errors from IBM Q, aiming to enhance the protocol's applicability to diverse practical use cases. Moreover, our CVQC protocol has been successfully demonstrated in front of an actual classical verifier. Our research shows that the accuracy of CVQC can be enhanced by approximately $93\%$ through fine-tuning its NN model, requiring at most an additional $10^3$ labeled samples from truly random states for training. Our results indicate the potential of integrating machine learning with classical and quantum computing, potentially accelerating the verification process by an order of magnitude, with further optimization likely to yield substantial gains. Our research, presented here, serves as an initial step in uncovering the interplay between quantum algorithms and classical ML models, opening up novel avenues of research in this rapidly developing, yet still relatively understudied, field. A blockchain system's consensus algorithm plays a crucial role in ensuring the integrity of the chain by resolving potential conflicts and enabling more advanced functionalities. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel energy-efficient consensus algorithm, known as LC4IoT, which reduces communication waste and minimizes the energy consumption and delay associated with executing specific contract functions. Our experimental results demonstrate that LC4IoT outperforms existing consensus algorithms by providing low latency, energy efficiency, and increased throughput. The proposed consensus algorithm can serve as a general solution for various blockchain applications, particularly those requiring low energy consumption and delay. The suitability of LC4IoT for mobile IoT networks can be inferred from its compliance with the energy-harvesting and self-sustaining properties specified in IEEE 802.11ad standard, which enables devices to operate independently without human intervention. The effectiveness of LC4IoT is further exemplified by its use in implementing a real-time IoT-based supply chain tracking system. To achieve efficient real-time tracking, we introduce a CSQ-based partitioning approach to facilitate location updates and queries. The approach allocates a specific geographic area to a blockchain user agent, enabling the quick propagation of location updates and queries within that region. For readers with print disabilities, particularly those with visual impairments, accessing complex scientific documents requires efficient navigation. Internal references in scientific papers allow readers to skip to related sections within the same document, but their full potential is realized when combined with visual content. This enables readers to understand the context of the reference by navigating to the corresponding section, but this benefit is lost when read electronically due to the inability to synchronize visual content. This study proposes a solution for print-disabled scientists by developing a vision-based technique that identifies and links references in scientific papers through image processing and machine learning. This approach involves three key components: (1) detecting section headings that match internal references; (2) identifying the correct reference among matching section headings; and (3) calculating the navigation target based on the identified reference. This method was tested using a corpus of 120 papers from the field of computer science and was compared with human performance in a subsequent study. Results showed that the technique accurately identified 82.7% of references with an average delay of 2.2 sections, closely matching human accuracy and navigation efficiency. This method has the potential to become an accessible feature in document readers, benefitting scientists with print disabilities by making their work more efficient. To facilitate this, a sample extension for LibreOffice and Chrome browsers was developed, demonstrating the potential for this technique to be implemented as an accessible feature. This sample extension allows users to automatically sync references between the document and their browser, enabling faster navigation. This sample extension was tested using the same corpus of 120 computer science papers, successfully syncing 75.8% of references. Users with print disabilities can access this sample extension through the website. In the future, this technique could be integrated into document management systems or scholarly communication platforms as an accessible feature, significantly benefiting users with print disabilities. To facilitate seamless adoption, this approach should be implemented as an author-level feature, allowing authors to make their work more accessible to print-disabled readers. Moreover, this technique has broader implications, enabling researchers to collect valuable data on how readers navigate documents in both physical and digital environments, particularly in fields where document length varies significantly. Finally, this technique's potential is not limited to print-disabled readers, as it could also benefit users who prefer to focus on specific sections of the document, allowing them to adjust the navigation targets accordingly based on their personal preferences. With further refinement, this technique could be applied across various document types, including academic manuscripts, books, conference proceedings, and legal documents, potentially increasing readability and accessibility for a broader range of users.

We investigate the case of HD189733b, a strongly irradiated planet whose light curve has been influenced by various factors such as its own emission patterns, the effects of its host star, atmospheric particles, and atmospheric gases (O$_2$, H$_2$O, CO). By analyzing high-resolution spectra taken through the HARPS-N telescope paired with low-resolution transit data, we strive to isolate individual influences on this planet's light curve, particularly the light curves of individual nights and composite spectra. We utilize the P2P method, originally designed for simultaneous analysis of light curves and spectra, and successfully reproduce the observed light curves with reasonable accuracy in HD189733b's early data sets, albeit with inconsistencies in later data sets due to increasing noise levels. We estimate a 1 in 5 chance that this replication is coincidental and attribute the discrepancies largely to atmospheric variability. Moreover, we identify the contributions of atmospheric gases (O$_2$, H$_2$O, CO) and the effects of its host star, and set an upper limit to the atmospheric particles' radiative time constant. This study showcases the effectiveness of combining high-resolution spectroscopy from HARPS-N with low-resolution transit data, and demonstrates that HARPS-N is capable of making valuable contributions to exoplanetary science by providing valuable constraints on the characteristics of planets and their host stars through detailed analysis of their light curves and atmospheric gases. To model these phenomena accurately, our approach involves seamlessly integrating downscaling techniques from coarse-grained ocean models that span deep into the open waters of the Pacific Ocean all the way down to the finer details of coastal inundation. To achieve this goal, a versatile adaptive simulation framework is employed. This flexible framework facilitates the iterative process of refining models in both time and space, effectively condensing complex tsunami data from coarse-grained models while generating the high-resolution data necessary for life-saving evacuations or structural damage assessments in coastal areas. In our study, we validate the efficacy of the adaptive simulations by leveraging a well-documented tsunami event: the 2011 Tohoku earthquake tsunami, for which a range of high-fidelity model data is available. We demonstrate the potential of the adaptive simulations to produce accurate results by directly comparing them with their corresponding high-resolution model counterparts. Furthermore, to highlight the importance of accurately modeling tsunami waves at varying scales, a simple numerical experiment is conducted. This experiment reveals a noticeable underestimation of coastal inundation depths if a high-resolution model of the open ocean is directly applied to the coastal region of the impacted areas, as exemplified by the city of Kesennuma. In conclusion, our research emphasizes the critical role of downscaling techniques in creating realistic tsunami scenarios by bridging the profound spatial and temporal scales inherent to these natural phenomena. To facilitate future breakthroughs in tsunami modeling, our code is now openly accessible and readily available for public use. To access our code, please visit the following repository: https://github.com/berkeley-labs/adaptivesim/tree/main/tukakaeki. Lastly, our approach highlights the potential of an iterative refinement process to effectively bridge the inherent scales of tsunami phenomena, effectively from deep ocean to coastal inundation. To achieve this goal, our research demonstrates the use of the Modest Tool Box, a versatile light-weight programming library that supports high-quality simulations of complex radiative transfer phenomena, including absorption, scattering, and emission. This tool box has previously been successfully applied to a diverse range of optical phenomena, as described in previous studies. In our current application, the Modest Tool Box is extended to accommodate tsunami simulations, effectively incorporating water surface elevation, average water depth, and flow profiles simulated by coarse-grained ocean models into the high-resolution simulations of the coastal region. To achieve this convergence, our simulations incorporate cutting-edge wave interactions, water level modulations, and flow dynamics, as modeled by the SCHISM software framework

PBLR was utilized in an empirical evaluation, revealing beneficial effects on its design and maintainability. Through our analysis, we reduced the side-lobe contamination that affects polarization measurements. Our analysis covered 149,964 point sources, of which 11,487 exhibited measurable polarization. We found the incidence of excess sidelobes in our data set to be satisfactory at around 4 percent and identified methods to minimize side-lobe interference in future data analysis. We discovered that about 6 percent of sources had significant polarization measurements, while 11 percent of sources displayed orientation self-correlation. We discovered no significant correlation between the curvature of the low-frequency radio background and the median polarization of sources. However, we found the median polarization of sources to be linked to the frequency, with a correlation coefficient of -0.65. We discovered significant upper limits for the characteristic curvature of the background polarization. Based on the data, we estimated an upper bound for the degree of polarization of sources at around 3 percent at 85 MHz. A new method to determine potential parameters has been developed for use in elastic particle scenarios where long-range potentials are dominant. In contrast to conventional methods, which rely on a direct comparison of measured data to calculated distributions, this approach involves a iterative process to identify the best-match potential. A novel feature of this new method is its ability to handle incomplete datasets, and can be applied to both radial and non-radial cross-sections with equal ease. A testing demonstration using simulated data showed that this approach can accurately pinpoint potential parameters even when there is a significant amount of noisy or missing input data. Furthermore, this approach was verified using real datasets obtained from laser elastic particle scattering experiments. A comparison of the results obtained using the new method showed agreement with those predicted using a maximum likelihood method on the order of 10 times more precise, while also revealing the presence of a non-zero spin potential. A thorough investigation using all available experimental data also yielded potential parameters that matched the results obtained using the new method, underscoring the effectiveness of this approach. A publicly accessible version of the code used in the new method has been made available online. A related code repository that contains the code and simulated data can be accessed at https://github.com/FernandoVega-Guilde/PotentialFitting, while the research paper detailing the results of the real particle experiments can be found at doi:10.1016/j.physleta.2020.115981. Protecting user privacy in location-based services has become a top priority due to growing concerns over data security breaches. The problem of privacy loss when utilizing a single database is well-understood, however, no effective solutions have been developed to address situations where data dependencies come into play. In an effort to address this gap, we have created a framework that makes it possible to achieve differential privacy in the context of conditionally dependent data. The framework relies on a fundamental building block that utilizes Gaussian noise to mask private data and is applicable across various types of databases. Additionally, we have developed an analysis of privacy loss and an algorithm design that is memory-efficient, thus minimizing computational overhead. The efficacy of this approach was demonstrated in a real-world scenario involving DBLP conference data and location-based services such as finding influential users and recommended neighbors. The results show that our method achieves a balance between preserving data utility and ensuring user privacy. The application of our framework to these recommended neighbors resulted in a significant 71.43% reduction in over-alliance users without sacrificing any of the system's effectiveness. The method's broader implications and potential applications in various data streams are also explored. The study demonstrates how the proposed framework can be used to address challenges associated with privacy loss in multiple location-based services, including social networks, influence networks, and recommended neighbors, all while maintaining a reasonable level of system performance. The structure and function of brain networks can be distinguished in different states like awake vs. sleep. Research has largely overlooked how inter-site brain differences affect findings from studies analyzing functional connectivity. To address this gap, we investigated the impact of inter-site brain differences on individual and group distinction using resting-state fMRI data from 784 awake subjects. We discovered that inter-site effects significantly influence individual distinction, especially at distant brain sites. To account for these effects, we adapted a network analysis method. Our results show that this approach significantly enhances both individual and group distinction. Furthermore, we found that inter-site effects are a significant source of variability in brain data and should not be overlooked. Overall, our research highlights the importance of considering inter-site brain differences in network analysis. We propose an adaptive strategy that adjusts to inter-site effects to create a reliable prediction model for functional networks. We believe that our research will inspire novel methods for analyzing brain networks. It has broad implications for understanding brain function and can lead to the development of data-driven algorithms for various applications, such as neuroscience and computer vision. In a basic communication scenario with multiple stations that have access to unlimited private data, we explore the fundamental naming and counting issues. Our main goal is to understand how the energy used in solving these problems grows with the size of the system. Despite having no restrictions on the way the data is constructed, we develop algorithms that work efficiently within limited resources. For instance, we can identify the largest number with $O(n/\log^2 n)$ energy if each station only knows a fraction of the numbers, while naming any element requires $O(n^{1/6} \log^2 n)$ energy if each station knows a unique string from a large set. We then discuss how these energy complexities match the lower bounds for these problems. Furthermore, we find that solving these problems in a more complex distributed setting, where separate channels are available for sending and receiving, leads to significant energy savings. Specifically, we can identify the largest number with $O(n^{1/4} \log^2 n)$ energy if each station only knows a fraction of the numbers, while naming any element requires $O(n^{1/16} \log^2 n)$ energy if each station knows a unique string from a large set. We achieve these results by designing energy-efficient algorithms that take advantage of the properties of this distributed setting. Moreover, we find that solving these problems in a more centralised setting, where a central point processes the data, leads to significant energy savings. Specifically, we can identify the largest number and counting any element requires $O(n^{1/4})$ energy if each station only knows a fraction of the numbers, while naming any element requires $O(n^{1/2})$ energy if each station knows a unique string from a large set. We achieve these results by designing efficient algorithms that take advantage of the data structure constructed during the distributed setting. Our findings show that the energy used in solving these problems grows slowly with the size of the system. Researchers have employed precomputed trajectories to enhance real-time motion planning efficiency, particularly in complex environments. The key issue lies in generating an optimal set of precomputed trajectories. Current methods often rely on random sampling or heuristic search, resulting in either under- or over-sampling of the state space, thus failing to reach optimal performance. This paper seeks to address this limitation by introducing a novel sampling method based on spatial constraint filtering to minimize state space exploration errors. The proposed method initially derives spatial constraints from a configuration space grid, then employs these constraints to generate prioritized sampling sites. The site with the highest priority is selected and used to initialize a trajectory via an adaptive search algorithm, ultimately supplementing the existing trajectory set. The proposed approach has been thoroughly evaluated using two simulation tools, namely, the Planning in Helicopter Navigation (PHN) benchmark and the Gazebo robotics benchmark. Compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods, the proposed method exhibits a 30% reduction in the number of precomputed trajectories required to achieve optimal performance, with a corresponding improvement of 20% in execution time. The results of this study show that the proposed method outperforms existing approaches and offers a promising framework for future research. This research focuses on identifying and categorizing a specific type of Markov process that exhibits unique quasi-stationary characteristics, converges exponentially to a specified distribution, and meets certain irreducibility requirements. A key finding demonstrates that a Markov process with a distribution that exhibits a natural exponential convergence is inherently quasi-stationary. Conversely, a Markov process with a distribution that converges subexponentially is not necessarily quasi-stationary. This discovery leads to the creation of a new class, denoted Q1, consisting of Markov processes possessing a distribution that converges exponentially and meets specific irreducibility requirements. This paper focuses on how these flavor-symmetric confining vacua solve the 't Hooft anomaly matching equations in order to demonstrate their stability. This approach is applied to various chiral gauge theories, including those with adjoint and bi-adjoint matter, as well as a special case where a fundamental matter field breaks the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry. For each case, we identify the minimum set of operators required to match the 't Hooft anomaly, leading to the discovery of new confining vacua which cannot be achieved through RG flow between different phases with the same matter content. Furthermore, our results imply a more precise definition of phase transitions in chiral gauge theories where the 't Hooft anomaly remains unchanged. This work sets a standard for precise description of confining vacia in chiral gauge theories, implying a more restrictive criterion on the stability of confining vacia. It also sheds light on an open question in relation to orientifolds, i.e. can a type-II string theory with a non-supersymmetric axio-dilaton field always stabilize all the fields in the spectrum in a confining phase when the axio-dilaton field cannot be absorbed into the gauge flux. We show in this paper that it is possible for confining phases to be unstable in some specific instances. For example, we identify an example where a confining phase can be unstable in an orientifold of $E_8\times SU(N)$ against an $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry exchange in both the $E_8$ and $SU(N)$ groups. This research investigates the thermal behavior of magnon complex systems, specifically targeted YbFeO$_3$, with features of antiferromagnetism and spin-oral disorder. Using inter- and intra-sublattice interactions, the magnon spectrum of this material is calculated through a self-consistent framework, incorporating temperature-dependent terms that result in the emergence of a temperature-controlled magnon bandgap. Further calculations demonstrate how this bandgap undergoes displacement as a function of wave transfer within the unit cell, yielding multiple magnon modes that independently arise according to the interaction types present. By applying the linear-spectroscopic theory of magnetization, the saturation magnetic order is calculated as a function of applied magnetic field and temperature, showing a pronounced shift due to interaction effects. Moreover, the theory enables determination of resonant modes that couple with external acoustic waves, revealing their respective frequencies and associated Q-values through conservation of momentum and dissipation mechanisms. Oral-spin-magnon and magnetic-moment-magnon interactions are identified as primary sources of resonant coupling, with magnon-magnon interactions exhibiting lesser significance. Numerical calculations also reveal significant magnon-magnon interactions at higher temperatures, producing a reversal in resonance modes according to the interaction effects present. Notably, the presence of spin-oral disorder has a profound impact on thermal behavior - it causes a widening of resonant modes and associated frequency shifts, resulting in the emergence of breakdown of Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equations. This material-specific finding implies that YbFeO$_3$ could serve as a unique example of a potential thermorheological device, with unidirectional heat dissipation via the creation of a backward magnon mode. This phenomenon could further enable the attainment of ultra-low energy states, previously proposed in antiferromagnets exhibiting spin-oral disorder. Moreover, the material could potentially undergo a unique phase transition, characterized by the emergence of a vanishing magnon bandgap as temperature increases. This phenomenon could further be marked by the absence of magnon resonance modes, resulting in the observation of a temperature-controlled magnon system. The findings presented serve as a starting point for the investigation of unique magnon systems, unique phases, and potential applications in the development of devices utilizing acoustic-magnetoelastic interactions. The proposed modifications result in a 20% reduction in public-key size and a 30% decrease in information transmission rates when compared to the original DHQKD system, however, this reduction leads to a significantly enhanced secret key rate. This research proposes a collaborative multi-agent learning approach for helping urban centers develop effective strategies for mitigating terrorist attacks by sharing security information. Through a dynamic interactive learning process, we examine various aspects of terrorist attacks on urban areas, including targets, time, and method of attack. Agents represent city agencies and make resource allocation decisions, with their ultimate goal of reducing urban area vulnerability to terrorist attacks. We introduce a new interaction topography, where urban areas host security information agents, and this structure influences how agents learn and interact within urban development scenarios. To assess the effectiveness of this multi-agent learning approach, we applied regression-based performance metrics to evaluate various learning techniques across different urban development scenarios, using case studies in Boston and Chicago to validate our approach. Ultimately, this multi-agent learning framework enables urban areas to develop effective strategies for preventing and responding to terrorist attacks by allocating resources and enhancing overall urban resilience. This research builds upon previous studies in sampling techniques for bag modeling and expands the findings to apply to long form content. We introduce two innovative bag sampling approaches - Incremental Bag Sampling and Sliding Window Bag Sampling - designed specifically for long documents. Our experimental evaluation incorporates publicly available datasets from LinkedIn search and YouTube order videos. The results demonstrate that both proposed methods effectively model bag semantics and enhance ranking performance. Notably, Incremental Bag Sampling achieves comparable performance to Sliding Window Bag Sampling while being well-suited to environments involving high latency and real-time updates. Furthermore, we combine the generative nature of adversarial networks with bag sampling to greatly reduce training time and improve long document ranking efficiency. This research is expected to accelerate the development of long document ranking on large-scale search engines. We publicly release the model's code at https://github.com/lingkiye/Search-bag-LONG.
