Developed to structure implicit knowledge into explicit forms that can be learned by models, the dataset comprises over 200K human-provided descriptions of common sense, tripled in size compared to its predecessor. Following a crowd-sourced alignment process, the revised dataset harmonizes its structure with other leading commonsense knowledge resources, including GPT-2-PRG, GPT-3-PRG, GCSI, and Conceptt. Evaluation assessments of duplicate and sequential analyses indicate the revised dataset's enhanced reliability. With the aid of human evaluators who compared descriptions to actual movie plots, the dataset was further human-tested for its coherence and relevance. When utilized in training models with descriptions from its competitors, ATOMIC 2020 proved itself to be the superior choice according to metrics such as accuracy and fluency in common sense-based reasoning tasks. You can access the revised ATOMIC 2020 dataset at https://www.kaggle.com/deshraj/atomic-2020. Evaluation code can be found at https://github.com/deshraj/atomic-2020-evaluation. A basic analysis framework is developed to investigate the speed-accuracy trade-off in one-dimensional physical systems. This model examines the diffusive dynamics of a target variable in the phase space of a given system, using the means square displacement measure. We provide a practical method to determine the speed-accuracy trade-off curve for any physical system, thus offering an valuable tool for system design. Our approach is illustrated through a physical evaluation of the optimal strategy in the case of resistive heating. Furthermore, a speed-accuracy trade-off curve is derived for a specific example, showcasing the impact of different rules for updating the control parameters on the performance. This study discusses the fundamental limitations that restrict the speed-accuracy trade-off, which are inherent to the physical system in question. We propose an efficient algorithm to numerically compute the optimal speed-accuracy trade-off curve and provide a straightforward analytical expression for this curve. Interestingly, this trade-off curve exhibits a distinctive feature, where the control parameters exhibit stochastic local equilibrium at a finite time. This peculiar aspect stems from the one-dimensional nature of the system under investigation. We also offer physical interpretations of the speed-accuracy trade-off curve to investigate the consequences of this phenomenon. Specifically, in the context of resistive heating, we discover that the means square displacement of the control parameters follows a straight line, characterized by an slope of 1/3. This value aligns with recent experimental findings (M. A. van den Noort et al., New J. Phys. 19 023045, 2017). We demonstrate that the speed-accuracy trade-off curve can be used to investigate different optimization strategies. In the case of resistive heating, for instance, we examine the features of local equilibrium during the optimization process. In addition, we discuss the distinctive feature of the speed-accuracy trade-off curve, which can be related to the occurrence of local equilibrium during the optimization process. Ultimately, we discuss the potential applications of the speed-accuracy trade-off curve, which can serve as a valuable benchmark for optimizing physical system design. Specifically, we compare the speed-accuracy trade-off curve with the optimal speed-accuracy trade-off curve, which are both plotted against the optimized value of $\gamma$ for different values of $\varepsilon$. As expected, the speed-accuracy trade-off curve provides a good estimate of the optimal speed-accuracy trade-off curve, except for large values of $\varepsilon$. When the system is far from the optimal regime, the speed-accuracy trade-off curve can serve as a useful design tool

Two notable thought experiments in the foundations of quantum mechanics, Frauchiger-Renner's setup and Hardy's setup, were initially considered incompatible with any quantum mechanical interpretation that adheres to Bayes' rule. However, it is now demonstrated that when applied in a quantum context, Bayes' rule can effectively resolve these paradoxes. The demonstration relies on a probabilistic interpretation that attributes measures to quantum states, rather than density operators. While the proposed method successfully reconciles the apparent contradictions, it does come with restrictions on how these measures can be used, particularly in the context of Hardy's setup. The reconciliation highlights the importance of specifying the domain of applicability of Bayes' rule in order to avoid falling into these fundamental inconsistencies. Conversely, it is also shown that when applied within its designated domain, Bayes' rule can serve as a valuable tool in evaluating the consistency of quantum theory. The importance of particular input assumptions regarding the quantum strategy is also emphasized in the context of Hardy's setup. The analyses further reveal that the application of Bayes' rule in the presence of quantum theory is particularly adept at handling tasks within the realm of causal inference. The study ultimately indicates that while the paradoxes may reveal flaws in naive implementations of Bayes' rule in the quantum setting, they do not necessarily constitute insurmountable obstacles to deriving useful information from quantum theory. The provided insights may find use in areas such as the application of machine learning in quantum systems, which is discussed in the conclusion. A related repository containing additional information is available at https://github.com/arjun-philosopher/quantum-bayes. A previous version of this study, incorporating crucial corrections regarding the application of Bayes' rule in Hardy's setup, was posted as arXiv:2101.09060. The current paper significantly expands on that work. The original paper is an extension of arXiv:1803.10485, which resolved the Hardy paradox. The interaction between autonomous agents in distributed control systems is often limited by communication, leading to a compromise between the agents' ability to perform tasks efficiently and effectively. To overcome this challenge, researchers have explored the application of game theory to optimize communication strategies, focusing on either minimizing costs or achieving better performance. To address this paradox, this paper presents an adaptive approach that enables agents to balance both goals, achieved by modeling the win-loss dynamics of players in evolutionary games. We test our model using a variety of game scenarios, including the Linear Time-Invariant time-delay system, to validate its predictive power and flexibility. Our findings reveal that this approach can successfully identify key game parameters, such as payoffs and noise levels, even under uncertain conditions. Furthermore, we show that our model accurately forecasts the outcomes of different game scenarios, including different architectures and games. To validate its practical applications, we use the game parameters identified by our model to devise an adaptive communication strategy that improves the performance of a fuzzy controller in a continuous path autonomous vehicle system, ultimately leading to better results than when communication costs are maximized. With its potential for wide applicability, we suggest that our model can be applied to various scenarios to optimize the trade-off between communication costs and effectiveness in various distributed control systems. We also outline future research avenues to expand the applicability of our model to different domains. To facilitate its use, we provide an open-source implementation of our model, available at https://github.com/alejdev/evolutionary-games. We hope that this resource will serve as a foundation for researchers to address the complex issues of distributed control systems. To enable the application of our model to control systems, we provide an open specification of the Essential Input Specification, defined by ISO 9241-20, through an XML file that outlines the required information to analyze the application of our model to different domains. We believe that making our model available in an easy-to-use format will facilitate its use by researchers to address the paradox of distributed control systems. Most image search algorithms face challenges with image copy detection problems, such as noise robustness and efficient query acceleration. To overcome these issues, we propose the DactiveHash algorithm. This method converts image features into compact vectors by synthesizing DCGAN-generated images at different stages and combining them with saliency maps. The vector representation enables fast comparison of query images across multiple angles to improve detection accuracy and resistance to modifications. The effectiveness of DactiveHash has been proven through comprehensive experiments and benchmark evaluations, showcasing enhanced robustness and efficient processing capabilities. Additionally, our method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in image search tasks, as demonstrated by the open-source code and pre-trained models shared publicly. Furthermore, we introduce an innovative image search interface that allows users to quickly find relevant images by specifying the expected modifications. The proposed interface provides users with the ability to directly ask the model about specific image transformations, such as watermarks, orientations, or compositions, as well as the range of possible changes. This user-friendly search interface leverages the DactiveHash method's capability to simulate image generations and perform queries based on the specified modifications. As such, the proposed image search system is termed DactiveHash. The source code and pre-trained models shared publicly enable other researchers to build similar systems based on the DactiveHash method. Overall, the DactiveHash method aims to contribute to the open research community and aid in image search algorithm development. The algorithm's open-source code and pre-trained models shared publicly enable other researchers to build similar systems based on the DactiveHash method. The long-term behavior of discrete-time Brownian motion in periodically varying, straight potential profiles is the focus of this investigation. Around one specific potential profile that resembles the periodized form of the already well-understood Alice in Wonderland scenario, we find that the distribution of particle locations converges towards a stationary state characterized by an infinite velocity sensitivity, indicating superdiffusive behavior with an exponent of 2. Conversely, in a different potential profile that is also periodized but not topologically equivalent to the Wonderland scenario, we show that the distribution of particle locations, after a long time, asymptotically converges towards a Gaussian distribution with a mean that varies randomly over time according to a Brownian motion curve, a phenomenon we've dubbed "diffusive chaos" in discrete-time Brownian motion. Despite both scenarios being discrete-time versions of diffusion processes, "diffusive chaos" has no direct analogy to them. We also explored discrete-time versions of other diffusion processes with periodic variants. For periodized versions of the Smoluchowski scenario, we found evidence of normal diffusion. However, for periodized versions of the standard diffusion equation in any dimension greater than one, we discovered that the distribution of particle locations, after a long time, asymptotically converges towards the stationary solution of the spatial periodic variant, a phenomenon we've termed "quasi-stationarity" in discrete-time diffusion processes. We demonstrated that discrete-time Brownian motion, even though it has a finite mean lifetime, can still exhibit long-term behavior convergence to one of these three different limits, depending on its starting position. Consequently, in discrete-time versions of diffusion processes, there may be a long-term behavior even for processes that do not reach their limiting distributions, and we called this phenomenon "long-term behavior convergence" in discrete-time diffusion processes, even when the process does not converge towards a limiting distribution. Discrete-time versions of diffusion processes can display complex temporal dynamics, and we concluded that discrete-time versions of periodic diffusion processes may display more intricate temporal behaviors than their continuous-time counterparts. In discrete-time Brownian motion with tilted periodic potentials, we found temporal periodicities that vary depending on the starting position and observed an infinite velocity sensitivity, indicating superdiffusive behavior with an exponent of 2. In discrete-time versions of diffusion processes with periodic variants, long-term behavior convergence typically implies temporal periodicities that vary depending on the starting position, except in discrete-time versions of diffusion processes with periodic variants that do not exhibit normal diffusion, where these periodicities vary only slightly depending on the starting position. We investigated the impact of a significant financial shock on the real economy. Utilizing a vector autoregression model, we discovered that moderate financial shocks have a minimal, short-term effect on the real economy, primarily influencing stock and credit markets. Conversely, extreme financial shocks yield distinct results - shocks originating from the equity market have a detrimental impact, whereas those stemming from credit markets have a beneficial effect on real GDP. Furthermore, we found that consumers and firms adjust their spending and saving habits in response to financial shocks by reevaluating their stock holdings and adjusting their consumer debt. We discovered that over a two-year period, the effect of extreme financial shocks on real GDP can be as high as 1.5% and 1.7%, respectively. Ultimately, we concluded that the magnitude and type of financial shocks play a pivotal role in determining their influence on the real economy. To mitigate economic damage, we recommend directing monetary and fiscal policies towards specific goals - a credit-based shock calls for increased borrowing to stimulate growth, whereas a equity-based shock demands an emphasis on debt restructuring and reduced interest rates to alleviate borrowers' financial burdens. We observed that the 2007 equity financial shock and the 2019 credit shock correspond to the phenomena of sub-prime mortgage crisis and global trade tensions, respectively. Consequently, implementing targeted policies could yield considerable economic benefits, quantitatively aligning with our predictive models' forecasts. Notably, the economic recovery following an equity-based shock could present opportunities for policymakers to harmonize regulations to benefit all stakeholders, whereas a credit-based shock can be mitigated through interest rate adjustments. In practice, the economic effects resulting from our proposed policy interventions amount to 2.0% and 2.2% for equity and credit shocks, respectively. To validate the economic influences, utilizing a Monte Carlo simulation to forecast growth enabled us to accurately anticipate and quantify the economic impacts stemming from the 2007 equity and 2019 credit shocks. Ultimately, the economic damages resulting from these shocks amount to -8.0% and -9.0% for equity and credit shocks, respectively. We validated our model's accuracy by comparing its forecasted outcomes to real-world economic phenomena. Specifically, the -5.0% predicted decline in the 2007 equity shock and -5.0% predicted growth in the 2019 credit shock correspond to the -37.0% peak decline in the 2008 stock market and 2.0% growth in the 2009 economy, respectively. This research paper addresses the problem of scheduling multiple virtual machines (VMs) within a multi-VM environment, where each VM is assigned multiple, potentially unequal-sized Logical Processors (LPs). The main goal is to effectively distribute real-time LP requests from multiple-protocol level entities to suitable physical machines (PHs) and then map the requested LPs to available Physical Processors (LPs) on chosen PHs. The proposed scheduling approach, called Prepartition, enhances resource allocation by pre-allocating resources based on request prefixes, thus ensuring more efficient and balanced scheduling. The method involves establishing a log to keep track of allocated resources and a database to store pre-allocated prefix schedules. The Prepartition method ensures the establishment of a scalable and balanced log by examining the request prefixes to forecast multiple-level protocol entity demands. The effectiveness of the Prepartition method was verified through mathematical modeling and simulation, demonstrating its capability to adapt to changing workload patterns. The simulation also revealed that the Prepartition method outperforms traditional binary search and dynamic heap allocation by significantly reducing scheduling overhead while ensuring low and balanced log loading. The outcome shows that the Prepartition method is suitable for dynamic and multi-level scaling and can be applied to various distributed real-time systems, including communication systems, databases, and cloud environments. The method particularly demonstrates its applicability in social media networks, such as Twitter, characterized by bursty and self-similar workload patterns with significant multiple-level communication demands. The method's scalability and efficiency were validated using a Twitter-like workload simulation, demonstrating its ability to handle a large number of requests and distribute them among available machines. Normal users can view public information, followee users gain access to some private information and interact with other users through publishing and commenting, while publishers can post information and engage with other users via mutual publishing. The proposed model incorporates two main components: a value estimation layer that ensures fixed-point convergence and branch prediction units that facilitate the identification of various solution equilibria. Experimental comparisons across several games demonstrate N-FPNs' ability to outperform existing approaches, including NFGPNs, while showcasing greater efficiency than generic neural network architectures. Notably, N-FPNs' adaptive learning process results in more stable and balanced solution equilibria compared to baseline models. Furthermore, model evaluations on Stackelberg games indicate that N-FPNs' output can be effectively utilized as Stackelberg equilibria by positioning them as upper-layer networks. Finally, the research identifies key challenges in modeling complex games with numerous action or state spaces and suggests potential future directions for overcoming these hurdles. The proposed model, according to our analysis, presents a reasonable compromise between these opposing constraints. Automatic document summarization is the process of condensing lengthy written works into concise, readable summaries. Previous approaches to summarization typically relied on either extracting key points or paraphrasing sections, but often struggled with producing coherent, well-structured text. In this research, we present GAE-ISumm, an innovative model that leverages graphical representation and internal state propagation to simulate the human writing process. By employing Graph Attention to capture semantic relationships, GAE-ISumm generates high-quality summaries outperforming existing state-of-the-art models significantly. Notably, our model achieves a substantial boost in ROUGE-L F1 score of 21.2 points on the CNN/DailyMail dataset, one of the largest improvements recorded over previously proposed methods. Furthermore, GAE-ISumm's summaries exhibit improved logic, as evidenced by functional tests. The source code for GAE-ISumm is publicly available at https://github.com/asharakeh/GAE-ISumm. Our work offers a unique fusion of graph-based representation and sequential reasoning, opening new avenues for information extraction and document summarization. It also paves the way for understanding the link between human cognition and artificial intelligence via Graph Neural Networks. Ultimately, our research serves as an inspiration for uncovering the underlying mechanisms of human intelligence through reverse engineering. Our findings demonstrate empirically the efficacy of the simulated approach as a method for skill acquisition. As a testament to its capability as a knowledge reflection framework, GAE-ISumm achieved generalization by using only human-level performance as its goal, in line with the principles of cognitive robotics. In the near future, our model will be put to use in cognitive robotics by Asharakeh et al. [2023]. In addition to our empirical contributions, GAE-ISumm's design holds significance at a theoretical level, particularly in understanding the link between human cognition at an abstract, psychological level and artificial intelligence at an algorithmic, neural level. To facilitate further research, our work presents GAE-ISumm as an exemplar model based on graphs that integrate external knowledge with sequential reasoning, capable of producing high-quality summaries. The model is distinguished from previous studies not just in its performance metrics, but also in its ability to replicate the human writing process by utilizing both graph representation and state propagation. In this research, a detailed examination is conducted on the training methodology for the autoencoding portion of Variational Autoencoders, focusing on the trade-offs between minimizing the reconstruction loss and regulating the posterior distribution of the encoder. Two key aspects are investigated: Firstly, analyzing how the flexibility of the variational distribution impacts training and its effect on posterior distribution, where a flexible variational distribution facilitates a well-defined posterior distribution but may impede training. Secondly, evaluating the significance of posterior distillation at the commencement of training, where adjusting the posterior distribution has varying effects depending on the layer under investigation. As a result, two optimization algorithms are proposed, with or without distillation, to enhance VAE training and posterior distillation. Two subsequent studies reveal that these methods significantly improve posterior distillation and sampling efficiency while revealing interesting insights about the posterior distribution and its variation across layers. Furthermore, our research shows that adjusting the variational distribution is more effective than modifying the prior distribution, suggesting a need to reassess traditional training protocols for VAEs. To facilitate reproduction of our results, our code is publicly available at https://github.com/rima21/dist-vae-reanalysis. Additionally, we have contributed an improved version of the posterior distillation VAE to Pytorch-Light, https://pytorch-light.pytorchlight.io/v0.2.1/dist_vae.html. As an extension of this research, we have examined the possibility of improving model performance using distillation-based approaches, where notable results were obtained from the model representation rather than input data, an unexpected finding of this research. We have submitted a separate paper detailing our findings from this research, titled \textit{Distillation-based approaches for improving Variational Autoencoder performance}. We have also presented a more comprehensive analysis of our research at ECML-PKDD 2022, titled \textit{Distillation for Posterior Distribution and Sampling in Variational Autoencoders}. A cost-effective wireless communication technique widely adopted in smart home settings is Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE). Enabling device localization in home environments with BLE wireless access points (APs) is a key functionality for various applications, a capability that is currently unavailable in popular BLE standards. Our research focuses on developing an advanced device localization system utilizing received signal strength index (RSSI) based trilateration to estimate the location of BLE devices within a BLE-enabled smart home. Our solution leverages a multilayer neural network to map device location, a novel approach in the field. We evaluated the performance of our proposed RSSI and mapping-based localization methods during two wireless activity periods, using extensive data collected from 600 subjects across 5,400 in-home locations. Our study demonstrates that the proposed system can accurately identify central home locations for new test subjects, yielding an overall localization accuracy rate of approximately 71% at a precision of 1.5 square meters. Moreover, we discovered that the proposed system can accurately pinpoint a new test subject's location within smart homes, reaching an accuracy rate of 65% when using a single BLE signal. Our research provides the first trilateration and RSSI-mapping-based device localization system for BLE devices and opens up significant research avenues in BLE device localization, a crucial aspect of various IoT applications. A newly developed approach focuses on condensing embedding vectors in the last layer, yielding substantial improvements over existing methods in terms of compression ratio and accuracy. By integrating this pointwise quantization strategy with layer-by-layer folding and retraining, the proposed technique surpasses state-of-the-art results, achieving a mean average precision of 78.1% and 80.1% on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 datasets respectively with only 2 bits per parameter. Furthermore, the proposed method exhibits exceptional adaptability, enabling efficient pointwise quantization on diverse architectures such as ResNet50 and MobileNetV2. Importantly, the proposed method requires minimal retraining following the standard procedure, yielding high-quality results. Overall, the proposed method establishes new benchmarks for top-level neural network quantization. Deep neural networks are commonly used for classification tasks that utilize noisy labels, which can lead to unreliable results if left uncorrected. A solution to this problem is ensemble modeling, where multiple neural networks trained on the same data contribute to a collective classification outcome. However, ensemble modeling typically relies on perfectly trained individual neural networks, which is not feasible when dealing with noisy labels. In this research, a novel ensemble modeling framework called SoftEn, designed specifically for handling label uncertainty, is proposed. SoftEn utilizes neural networks to generate refined probability distributions that improve classification accuracy. By taking a probabilistic approach, SoftEn combines the continuous and discrete uncertainty in label space to produce a more accurate classification than individual models. SoftEn's theoretical analysis confirms its ability to enhance classification accuracy, which is substantiated by experiments using real-world datasets. Notably, SoftEn achieved a significant 22.6% error reduction on the CIFAR-10 dataset compared to standard neural networks. Furthermore, SoftEn's performance is compared favorably to existing methods for learning from noisy labels. In addition to the theoretical benefits, SoftEn's results on the semantic segmentation dataset CamVid reveal a 4.2% error reduction and 10% increase in Fermi Index on the evaluation metric'mean Fermi Index' compared to standard neural networks. These findings indicate that SoftEn's approach yields robust and reliable results in the presence of label uncertainty. Corresponding code for SoftEn can be found on the GitHub repository https://github.com/asharakeh/SoftEn.git. SoftEn's theoretical analysis and research results are presented in full detail in the supplementary document. This paper examines the behavior of transfer operators and their permutations in relation to correlation decay for semiflows with either uniform or non-uniform expansions. We utilize a novel approach based on the ergodic theorem to establish the distinct behaviors of these operators and then demonstrate how they exhibit different behaviors in dynamical systems such as non-uniformly expanding maps on intervals and partially hyperbolic systems. Furthermore, we illustrate the applications of this theory by investigating the spectral properties of these operators in certain dynamic systems. We reveal a particular property of partially hyperbolic systems under a small perturbation, namely, the transfer operators of the invariant manifold exhibit an exponential decay in correlations, whereas the transfer operators of the invariant manifold in certain non-uniformly expanding maps fail to exhibit such behavior. Lastly, we make a significant observation regarding the transfer operators in certain non-uniformly expanding maps, namely, for maps that exhibit an exponential decay in correlations, there exists a small neighborhood in which the transfer operators for all but one orbit converge exponentially to zero. Conversely, for maps that exhibit a polynomial decay in correlations, there exists a small neighborhood in which the transfer operators for all but two distinct orbits converge at a rate proportional to a polynomial and fail to converge exponentially. We conclude by highlighting some open questions related to transfer operators, particularly for non-uniformly expanding maps, which remain unresolved in the current literature. By applying a likelihood-based matching procedure to simulated data, they matched simulated $\bquark$ events with those from $\Lambda_b^0$ decays. This involved calculating the relative ratios of previously unseen $\Lambda_b^0$ decay processes by comparing their simulated and observed event counts. The study utilized four distinct $\Lambda_b^0$ decay methods: $K^-pK^+\pi^-$, $K^-p\pi^-\pi^+$, $\bar{K} e \nu_e$, and $p e \nu_e$. The researchers determined that four new $\Lambda_b^0$ decay channels showed rates consistent with predictions made by the parton package HOPSPOT, while ten such decay channels were found to have rates differing from those in HOPSPOT. The study also identified $\Lambda_b^0$ decay processes that could be used to measure $b$-quark fragmentation functions. The measured $b$-quark fragmentation functions were found to have lower values for $D^{0}\overline{D^{0}}$ and $u\overline{d}$ and, to a lesser extent, $c\overline{c}$ and $\gamma$ states compared to fragmentation functions predicted in HOPSPOT. Researchers have long debated whether student isolation in grades and performance is a necessary evil for their growth as programmers. In this study, we examined the impact of two anonymous grading tools on students' learning outcomes, using tools for dynamic feedback and static feedback in the same course over a span of three years. The course in question was an introductory computer science course with over 600 students spread across the two feedback sections. What constitutes "growth through isolation" remains a topic of debate, but for the purposes of this study, we defined it as the difference in program metrics and grades between the two feedback sections. Notably, we found that students receiving static feedback, which provides expected exam grades and a passing score in advance, exhibited "growth through isolation" in terms of code coverage but not programming grades. Conversely, students receiving dynamic feedback, which provides actual exam grades and a passing score in real-time, performed equally well in both code coverage and grades. It is worth noting that students receiving dynamic feedback scored higher than their static feedback counterparts, averaging an 8% higher score. It is also worth mentioning that students receiving dynamic feedback covered nearly 5% more code in their programs compared to those receiving static feedback. In an effort to shed light on this phenomenon from the instructors' perspective, we conducted post-experiment interviews, during which some instructors expressed concerns over the equity of the dynamic feedback method and requested the reinstatement of anonymous grades. Interestingly, however, we found that a significant number of students receiving dynamic feedback actually outperformed their peers in code coverage and grades, leading us to hypothesize that anonymous grading may have a negative impact on certain students' motivation and approach to programming. In an effort to explain this "growth through isolation" phenomenon, we posited several theories, including the role of intrinsic motivation in students receiving dynamic feedback, the anxiety and demotivation of students receiving static feedback, and the perceived lack of fairness in the dynamic feedback method. In an effort to expand on these theories, we examined the correlation between the dynamic feedback method and code coverage, program length, and grades in a subsequent course, during which we found a significant positive correlation with code length but no significant correlation with grades or code coverage. In an effort to validate these theories, we conducted post-experiment interviews with students, during which we found a significant number of students expressing anxiety, distrust, and a lack of motivation in students receiving static feedback. Interestingly, however, we found a significant number of students receiving dynamic feedback expressing confusion and a perceived lack of fairness in the dynamic feedback method

This research investigates how source data influence traditional domain adaptation methods when no source data are available in the target domain. Existing domain adaptation techniques rely on source data to learn a common feature space, but our study shows that they work as intended when there's a lack of source data. Consequently, these methods solely learn target data, resulting in suboptimal performance. We have developed a novel domain adaptation approach called "unsupervised domain adaptation without source data" (UWoS), which determines key target features and constructs an artificial source domain without any initial source data. The selected target features are then used to train a domain adaptation classifier. This research also explores the practical application of the UWoS approach to real-world, unsupervised scenarios. The fuel mixture inside a gas core reactor maintains its structural integrity due to external heat flux distribution.  High heat flux areas contain small fuel droplets that break down into gas state, which increases the local pressure.  This pressure rise creates convection currents that counteract, dissipating the heat flux.  As a result, gas core reactors can operate more efficiently with uniform heat distribution when the pressure increases in response to the heat input.  Therefore, GCAR can function effectively even with extremely high heat fluxes that would be detrimental to solid fuel reactors.  Current mathematical models of GCAR are inadequate, so an analysis of the mass conservation equation is conducted to determine the optimal mathematical representation for the mixture's density.  By making this adjustment, the model can accurately simulate the GCAR's operation, which has significant practical implications for developing and operating reliable power reactors.  Our study incorporates high-order methods of discretization, which enables an accurate simulation of the GCAR by capturing its turbulent convection currents.  By providing a precise solution to the GCAR problem, our method facilitates the evaluation of different fuel configurations as potential designs for power generation.  Our simulations of the GCAR can potentially be adapted to other nuclear power applications, such as fuel cooling systems or nuclear propulsion systems, which also experience convective currents.  These other systems are not the focus of our study, however.  By utilizing an operator splitting technique, our simulations take into account the effects of thermal conductivity, viscous forces, pressure gradient, and the presence of small droplets.  By assuming that the mixture's temperature, pressure, and droplet distribution remain uniform across the GCAR at its boundaries, our simulations accurately capture the turbulent convection currents within the reactor. We introduce a neural network, "4D-GenNet," capable of generating four-dimensional simulations of particle collisions. This simulation utilizes a modular architecture that incorporates prior knowledge from detectors, making it efficient and easy to implement within existing detector simulations. Compared to a conventional fully connected neural network, "4D-GenNet" achieves a notable speed boost in generating thousands of simulated events. Furthermore, we evaluate the capability of "4D-GenNet" to produce genuine-like events for the CMS detector operated during the LHC's Run 2. To assess its performance, we generate candidate events for a Z boson decaying into two leptons with a transverse momentum above 20 GeV, within a pseudorapidity range of |η| < 2.4 and less than 100% collision momentum. These events are then passed through a digital detector simulator replicating the CMS detector. "4D-GenNet" events are selected and compared to actual data collected during Run 2 in two metrics: event energy distribution in pseudorapidity and collision momentum, |dE_in/dη|, and event uniformity across significantly reduced event numbers, O(10^5). Remarkably, "4D-GenNet" maintains a maximum residual discrepancy of approximately 8.3%, staying within experimental uncertainty of real data. To validate its reliability, we create "4D-GenNet" events within a pseudorapidity range of |η| < 5.2 and simulate the HL-LHC detector. Notably, this expanded simulation retains a general resemblance to actual data, maintaining a residual discrepancy below 15% across a broad energy range. To facilitate user-friendly generation of four-dimensional simulations, we provide the source code for "4D-GenNet" in a public repository. Additionally, detailed instructions for converting the CMS detector's geometry and hit-prediction models into a friendly format suitable for "4D-GenNet" are included. Although initially designed for the CMS detector, these conversion utilities can be applied to other detectors with minimal modifications. Furthermore, "4D-GenNet" events are proposed as a training dataset for unsupervised learning in detector development, due to their diverse range of complex, genuine-like events. Answer Set Programming (ASP) logic programs incorporate modules from external libraries, grounded using specialized algorithms, to address temporal and aggregate reasoning. However, the ASP semantics fail to account for aggregates containing nested constructs like before/11 or cumulative functions from external libraries, preventing these aggregates from being grounded. This limitation is alleviated by introducing a new semantics that facilitates the grounding of recursive aggregates. This approach modifies how variables are shared between modules to ensure consistency. Notably, the proposed semantics deviates from established ASP interpretations but aligns with developer intentions in scenarios like before/11 and cumulative examples. To rectify the existing semantics's insufficiency, we introduce a new variable sharing rule and demonstrate that using this approach for recursive aggregates does not lead to ungroundable aggregates. Finally, we assess the feasibility of implementing this approach using existing ASP systems and discuss potential issues that still require resolution. This research targets a comprehensive understanding of ASP's semantics for modular programs, contributing valuable insights to the field. To streamline the analysis, we primarily focus on aggregates in this paper, although the developed methodology can be applied to other modular features. Our findings suggest that all widely used ASP systems can, in theory, implement the proposed semantics. Nevertheless, we encountered two main obstacles: (i) the interaction between module sharing and aggregate evaluation, and (ii) the inability of current generators to handle recursive aggregates. To address the first issue, we outline a set of properties required for safe module sharing among aggregate-generating modules. Then, we adapt existing generators to accommodate recursive aggregates. Ultimately, we present groundings for two benchmark scenarios, illustrating that the proposed semantics lead to different models compared to the traditional interpretation of ASP's semantics. Moreover, we demonstrate that both the original and the proposed semantics can be implemented using a semantics-based approach, ensuring interoperability with existing generators. To facilitate a comprehensive understanding of ASP's semantics for modular programs, we provide aggregate-based benchmarks to aid developers in crafting suitable modules, thereby ensuring that the features of the language are utilized efficiently. On the other side, the benchmarks serve as criteria for assessing existing generators and highlight potential issues that still require resolution. Ultimately, we recommend adopting the proposed semantics as the new standard interpretation of ASP's semantics to ensure consistency and reliability. To facilitate this transition, we outline guidelines for developer-led implementations and forecast ASP's committee to make an official decision in the near future. We further anticipate that the integration of the proposed semantics into existing generators will alleviate the identified limitations, thereby bringing us closer to a comprehensive modular ASP language. Estimating essential information measures, such as mutual information, remains a difficult task for data scientists. Previous methods relied on discretizing data, dividing it into grid boxes, and calculating the entropy of the resulting probability grid. While simple, this approach can be effective. This paper presents a new method that builds upon moments of random variables to estimate important information measures, including mutual information. By utilizing only general assumptions about the probability density function, we derive a method that can be applied to any random variables without requiring a specific form for the density function. Additionally, we prove that using higher-order moments allows for more accurate estimates, given the same amount of data. This method's efficacy is demonstrated by comparing it to state-of-the-art methods for estimating mutual information in scenarios involving two variables. It shows comparable or slightly superior performance when given the same amount of data. However, our method excels by requiring significantly fewer data samples to achieve similar accuracy. Furthermore, we also utilize this approach to estimate conditional entropy and develop a method to calculate mutual information directly from time series data, avoiding the need to split it into segments. This improvement allows us to surpass previous methods in accuracy when given the same amount of data, while also being more suitable for time series data due to its higher efficiency. An implementation of the new approach can be found on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/cran/ComplexHeatMap/tree/master/HeatMapMI.R. A comprehensive comparison to other popular methods is conducted using well-documented datasets, such as those from the public Datasets4MI collection. Furthermore, we also release a Python package named HeatMapMI at https://github.com/pannenkoek55/HeatMapMI that allows for seamless estimation of mutual information relying solely on data samples, not requiring any prior knowledge about the probability density function. It integrates smoothly with popular data science tools like scikit-learn and can be utilized in both Jupyter Notebooks and Blender3D.  A comprehensive user guide, including step-by-step usage examples, can be found in Section 7. By combining our approach with visualization tools, we introduce ComplexHeatMap, a new method to effectively represent multivariate probability distributions, conditional entropies, and related information measures in an intuitive manner. An accompanying video illustrates the step-by-step process of calculating mutual information. We believe our approach makes significant contributions in the following areas: higher-order moments derivation, direct time series estimation, efficient visualization, and novel optimization. In higher-order topological insulators (HOTIs), even when disorder disrupts their band structure in the bulk, it often leaves intact the localized zero-mode states at the edges. However, this contradiction arises from the fact that our current understanding of hotspots, which are regions of enhanced disorder resistance, is limited to 2D systems, such as graphene. Therefore, we have adapted and expanded a method for activating edge modes that originally employed gate-voltage control in graphene hotspots to a 3D hotspots framework applicable to systems of any dimension. By applying this improved approach to HOTIs, we have discovered that the hotspots can activate bulk mobility at finite levels, bypassing the band-gap threshold typically required. Furthermore, we observed that the activated bulk mobility is linked not only to the size of the gap at the edges, but also to the number of layers in the HOTI structure, decoupling bulk mobility from the band gap in the process. Ultimately, we have identified that the hotspots can activate modes within the bulk that are disconnected from the edge states, which is a phenomenon that does not rely on the band-gap size. Consequently, we have made theoretical predictions for 3D HOTIs in the presence of various interlayer couplings, confirming that the activation of bulk mobility is robust across diverse coupling strengths. Acquiring high-quality images of non-transportable objects has long been a complex issue in computer vision. Given that traditional light field rendering techniques require a full set of images, researchers have focused on various machine learning-based solutions for capturing and reconstituting high-quality images. While initial machine learning-based approaches typically rely on numerous images at different angles, some researches have achieved notable results using only sparse images. This work is in the latter category. It addresses two key challenges: deriving geometric constraints from sparse images and incorporating these constraints into a realistic 3D scene reconstruction. The proposed method successfully merges two algorithms: one generates high-quality images from realistic 3D scenes and the other extracts geometric constraints from these scenes. Applying this method using only one image results in a 3D scene reconstruction that accurately replicates the object's appearance from new, unrealized viewpoints. Furthermore, this method enables users to edit certain aspects of the 3D scene before generating new images based on these changes. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through its ability to recover complex 3D scenes from a single view in some cases and from a few views in others with notable improvements resulting from the incorporation of geometric constraints. The method's real-world applications are diverse and include creating virtual decorations, editing and/or correcting 3D scenes, and recovering 3D scenes from images taken from a single point. Furthermore, existing research examples rarely utilize real-world sequential genetic data, which is a crucial area of exploration given genomics advancements and their implications for various diseases. To enhance the identification of significant variables and reduce computational load, we introduce a novel machine learning method, Relevance Learning Pathway (RLP), which integrates the study's purpose and variable correlations to predict genomic changes over time. By focusing on sequential genetic data, RLP effectively extracts meaningful variables from complex time-series data and reduces computational costs associated with conventional model analysis. In a comparative study using 16 datasets from the KDD Cup 2013 challenge, RLP consistently outperformed conventional model analysis in variable selection and predictive accuracy. Notably, RLP successfully utilized relevance learning to streamline the analysis of massive genomic data and demonstrate its practical applications in variable selection and predictive accuracy. Furthermore, RLP extracted meaningful variables from complex time-series data through an optimized analysis, resulting in a significant reduction in computational costs compared to conventional model analysis. The study's results suggest that RLP has the potential for a positive social impact in the field of bioinformatics. Research has discovered that RNNs trained through reinforcement learning or supervised control can sometimes overlook task requirements and act irrationally. We developed a theoretical framework for understanding the behavior of these neural networks in partially observable environments, incorporating the principles of dynamical systems and partial hidden Markov models. We found that when an RNN achieves optimal solutions, its hidden states evolve according to a dynamic system influenced by the task's optimal strategy. Since the RNN's learned behavior might not always align with the task's demands, we defined a metric for task-incompatibility, illustrating that even optimal solutions can be difficult for the RNN to attain due to the network's limited capacity for representation. We further investigated two common algorithms used for neural control: model predictive control and deep reinforcement learning, discovering that the first method can result in suboptimal outcomes similar to those obtained by the second method, where the RNN fails to achieve the task's optimal solutions. Our research highlights the need to balance the RNN's ability to learn from experience with its ability to adapt to changing environments, offering potential solutions to these problems. We demonstrated that our framework can serve as a diagnostic tool for understanding the behavior of which RNNs are capable and how they can be improved. We applied our theoretical framework to several control tasks, such as adversarial taxi dispatching and aerial surveying, to illustrate its practical applications to real-world challenges. We discovered that our framework can reveal RNNs' limitations in complex tasks and offer potential solutions to these problems. We demonstrated the practical implications of our framework by successfully modifying the air-broom system's parameters and adjusting the network architecture to allow it to achieve the task's optimal solutions. Our research laid out fundamental questions regarding neural reasoning and understanding, offering a theoretical foundation for addressing these critical issues. We offered publicly accessible code for our research on the online repository at https://github.com/jmjordao/RNNs-for-Optimal-Control. We concluded by highlighting several potential future research paths, suggesting that our framework can serve as a starting point for exploring these critical issues. Our proposed method integrates graph attention with graph convolutional neural networks to predict action detection in videos. 
This model treats video frames as nodes in a graph, where action labels are both predicted and linked to existing actions using attention coefficients.
To initialize node features, we combine encoder outputs from a two-dimensional convolutional neural network with a pre-trained object detection model.
Subsequent training of the proposed model enables the adaptation of node features from action-like features to more accurate action labels, and simultaneously maps related actions to one another.
This model is further differentiated based on its ability to localize action boundaries through the use of attention coefficients.
Experiments demonstrate that our method, K-GCN, outperforms existing approaches on the EPIC-KITCHENSCHALLENGE v1 and v2 datasets in multi-class action detection, particularly for class-aware detection tasks. The full implementation is available online at https://github.com/antonesc/KE-GCN. Ultimately, results indicate that action detection benefits significantly from object detection and graph attention mechanisms. This research paper proposes enhanced static filters to parameterized attacks, designed to counter a vulnerability in the WPA2 protocol that allows for exploitation using an attacker's MAC address. The proposed filters are capable of operating without the need for knowledge of future attacks, as they can be implemented using a device's connection history. Utilizing these static filters can prevent parameter attacks without compromising on speed, memory, and security. Recent advancements in end-to-end neural speech synthesis have improved significantly, yet highly natural speech production remains an unfulfilled goal. To bridge this gap, we suggest utilizing pitch-adjusted speech datasets during model training, as incorporating pitch variability enhances the controllability of synthesized speech. Two approaches are presented to implement this idea: the iterative augmentation method and the selective enhancement method. The former applies pitch modification to the entire training dataset, whereas the latter focuses on augmenting only non-standard pitch regions. The experimental outcomes confirm that incorporating pitch variability through the proposed methods leads to superior pitch controllability. Moreover, models trained with pitch-adjusted datasets demonstrate improved performance on tasks such as speech denoising and language transfer. It is observed that the selective enhancement method yields higher speech quality, greater variation in prosody, and higher speech evaluation scores (e.g., PESQ 4.7 vs. 4.6) compared to the iterative augmentation method. Furthermore, models produced using the proposed approach exhibit superior capabilities in unsupervised speech modification tasks, as observed in the speech denoising task where the PESQ score increases by 0.8. The experimental findings also reveal that increasing the degree of pitch adjustment within the selective enhancement method enables the mimicry of specific speaker characteristics, as verified by the speaker identification rate. At the highest degree of pitch adjustment, the closed-set speaker identification rate reaches 65%, thus establishing a novel application for the proposed approach. The discovery of multiple giant planets orbiting the same star has led scientists to question whether these planets could have originally merged or merged and separated, raising the possibility of mass convergence among them. However, different mass reduction mechanisms result in various mass-concentration patterns, and several theories about how multiple planets form remain debated. To clarify this, we conducted a series of simulations that model multiple planets accreting from the same disk, focusing on dispersal by disk companions and differential accretion. Our results show that differential accretion can lead to mass convergence among planets, and when disk companions are present, they can cause accreting planets to diverge in mass. Moreover, we found that when planets accrete at different rates, their masses converge to reflect their relative accretion rates. These outcomes match observations of exoplanetary systems, and multiple planets accreting simultaneously offers an explanation for mass convergence better than a single planet accreting multiple times, as it predicts varied outcomes in mass distributions. Building on this, we proposed an equation to approximate the mass ratio of accreting planets based on their relative accretion rates. Finally, we identified a boundary separating dispersal and differential accretion patterns in mass distributions, and further research is needed to examine the relative importance of these processes in shaping exoplanet mass distributions. With more data and better constraints on disk dynamics and planetary accretion, scientists will be better equipped to understand the formation and mass distribution of multiple exoplanets. As a result, theoretical models of planetary formation and mass ratios will likely need to be revised.

Research has shown that some parts of deep neural networks are better at adapting to new tasks than others, despite being trained on different data. A study examined the transferability of CNNs trained on ImageNet and tested it on VGG-Face recognition and Faster-RCNN object detection on the ImageNet dataset. It found that early layers, which learn basic image features, are not very transferable. This is likely because their parameters are specific to the initial training data and do not generalize well to new tasks. By contrast, mid-level layers, which extract more complex features, are highly transferable. Interestingly, late layers, which perform the final classification, are also transferable, possibly because they represent the most refined features of the input data. This study suggests that a key factor limiting the transferability of DNNs is the lack of shared features from the same domain between the training and test data. This can be mitigated by pre-training a CNN on relevant data and fine-tuning it on the target task. Additionally, using noise data during training can also enhance transferability. It is expected that future advances in this area will come from combining multiple self-supervised learning techniques. A public repository for the implementation of our method can be found at https://github.com/ylainn/transferability. Investigations into discrete-time channel models, employed for generating training data and labeling, have indicated that previously established models may not be highly accurate. This is particularly evident in cases where communication involves multiple hops, as evidence suggests that models are only accurate up to three hops ahead. To address this, we aim to determine which factors contribute to the inaccuracy of these models. Through a comprehensive analysis involving metrics such as average absolute linear correlation, Euclidean distance, and normalized Euclidean distance, we have developed a model that utilizes Gaussian processes to accurately predict channel impulse responses for arbitrary hop levels. We have found that these models can achieve correlation coefficients exceeding 0.95 for up to 21 hop levels, significantly outperforming impulse-based models which often fail for hop levels exceeding three. To further illustrate the effectiveness of our model, we have modified it to predict the distortion introduced by the channel when compressing information and have developed a model of the distortion coefficient using statistical regression. As a result, our model has achieved a coefficient of determination exceeding 0.95, demonstrating outperforming impulse-based models. To validate our models, we have set up a live testing system comprising 116 DMT-based homeplug AV2 modems connected over a network with up to 15 wireless hops. Owing to the versatility of our model, it can be easily extended to predict other characteristics of channels, such as frequency smoothing. Furthermore, we have developed a model capable of predicting the mean square error introduced by the channel when compressing information and have defined a model of the distortion coefficient using statistical regression. As a result, our model has achieved a coefficient of determination exceeding 0.95, demonstrating superior performance to impulse-based models. In contrast, robust learning techniques are designed to accommodate variations and uncertainties, utilizing a clean sample obtained from the data generating process, which can be used to train a non-robust model. The main objective of this research is to examine the existence of sumsets within countable abelian groups, specifically focusing on Bohr sets, and their expanded versions, known as generalized Bohr sets. This investigation builds upon previous findings by Ruzsa and the first author, as well as Tao, and involves a novel application of density-based approach that is potentially influential in solving other problems in sumsets. The existing lower density bound, posed by Ruzsa, is generalized to a higher density bound, $\overline{\rho}^*(A)$, which is called the upper Banach density. We demonstrate a near exact result showing that for any countable abelian group $G$ and subsets $A, B, C$ of $G$, if the upper Banach density of $A + B$ is positive, then a significant number of elements from the sumsets $A + B + C$ form Bohr sets. This breakthrough resolves a problem initially posed by Bohr in 1940 and later revisited by Ruzsa in 2011. The findings are complemented by examples illustrating that an "almost" precise outcome is inevitable, as well as an examination of sumsets' $\overline{\rho}^*$-uniformity. Subsequently, using the upper Banach density-based approach, we generalize the known results on Bohr set existence in abelian groups, potentially broadening their applications to combinatorial problems. The upper Banach density-based method enables us to verify that a sumset $A + B$ contains Bohr sets under a near-exact condition, and we leverage this principle to develop an optimized version of the generalized Khintchine inequality. We further explore the potential for generalizing theorems from the integers to specific classes of abelian groups, such as extensions of $\mathbb{Z}$. The upper Banach density-based method also facilitates discoveries on sets with distinct sum properties, known as $g$-ideals, and their expanded versions, known as $g$-ideals with expanded sum properties. Optimizing timetable optimization problems are addressed using a new method of path information utilization, which ensures high-quality solutions in near real-time for large transportation networks with hundreds of thousands of stops. The proposed algorithm identifies optimal times for starting and completing routes based on established paths while taking into account vehicles' current locations and operational environments. To achieve efficient processing, the problem is simplified by assuming fixed path information can be pre-processed, yielding a parameterized solution space. A computational method then iteratively applies parameters to produce high-quality starting points in a limited number of iterations. The algorithm is enhanced with asynchronous processing, allowing the system to quickly adjust parameters in response to changing conditions, with results demonstrated on a real-world bus reconfiguration problem within a commercial service for over 100 million customers. The algorithm consistently finds solutions within 0.1% of optimal quality in approximately 200-300 milliseconds, with the potential for substantial operational cost reduction through reduced vehicle usage. The algorithm's source code is also made publicly available on a public code repository for evaluation and validation. The research also examines the influence of path uncertainty on optimized solution quality, revealing a diminished impact when paths can be freely chosen but paths with flexible destinations substantially increase solution quality, highlighting a pressing need for research on path uncertainty in modern optimization applications. The study suggests this problem may be addressed using data-driven models to forecast passenger flow or incorporating probabilistic factors into path choice, with the latter offering significant potential for further exploration. The potential for leveraging passenger information systems to model uncertainty in passenger flow may also offer substantial value. Knowledge-based methods have gained significant attention in multi-modal learning, as knowledge modalities can mitigate the effects of unsupervised or unsupervable sensor data and enhance the robustness of multi-modal systems. Our proposed method employs graph-based knowledge models to integrate knowledge from various domains into multi-modal graph learning frameworks. This approach enables the construction of customised graph models for specific tasks and domain knowledge, allowing it to handle sensor data of any structure for multi-modal graph-based classification tasks. We propose a variational method to approximate the adiabatic gauge potential based on a reference wave function derived from a multiconfiguration Dirac-Hamiltonian, incorporating relativistic effects and electron-electron correlations. Our variational method involves computing key commutators related to the Hamiltonian, and we establish a relationship between variational parameters and the fluctuations of these commutators. We examine the performance of this method in valence double-configurations for hydride molecules, demonstrating its ability to accurately predict spectroscopic data. Furthermore, we adapt this method to compute an effective one-body Hamiltonian, incorporating important electron-electron interactions. Our revised algorithm eliminates the need for a reference wave function, instead initiating iterations from an arbitrary initial state. As a result, it can accommodate various wave functions, including multiconfigurational descriptions. We evaluate the efficacy of this method by comparing it to other efficient multiconfigurational approaches. Upon optimizing all parameters, it yields results comparable to perturbative corrections, yielding reliable estimates for spectroscopic data. We predict spectroscopic data for the Cs2 molecule, demonstrating that our method can accurately describe this weakly interacting dimer as a multiconfigurational system. We establish a set of benchmarks for spectroscopic constants based on a perturbative correction framework, showing that our method can attain this level of accuracy. Furthermore, we analyze the effect of variational parameters in different regimes and configurations, examining their fluctuations and correlations. We find that some parameters exhibit significant fluctuations across different configurations, suggesting the presence of essential correlations in certain regimes, often captured by multiconfigurational descriptions. We predict spectroscopic constants for isolated atoms, comparing our method's results to extensive basis-set calculations, and find a notable agreement with high-quality reference-sets. We find a notable agreement between our method's results and experimental data, particularly in the saturation regime, where our estimates reach an accuracy of a few hundredths of a wavenumber. We investigate how analyzing function representations, delivered by intermediate layers of neural networks, can enhance the readability of these models. Various studies have employed different approaches to extract these representations, but a unified explanation for their effectiveness is missing. Our research builds on previous findings, specifically regarding neural tangent kernels, which previous work found to yield superior results. In our study, we test this assumption with other methods, revealing that it's the kernelization step, not the tangent kernel itself, that significantly improves performance. Additionally, we discovered that applying kernelization after training, then combining the original network with random features from a Gaussian distribution, reaches comparable accuracy to methods applying kernels to input data beforehand. Interestingly, using tangent kernels for interpretability purposes often results in lower margin errors than methods utilizing deep nets, indicating that neural networks' readability largely stems from their ability to approximate kernel-based methods. Based on these observations, we propose a new approach: Train a neural network using Gaussian features, then discard its original weights, replacing them with a Gaussian distribution. This process provides theability to analyze representations through kernels without being confined by the original network's architecture. Our method allows feature extraction that matches or surpasses state-of-the-art interpretability results without being restricted by the original network's architecture. We tested our method's effectiveness across various margin classification problems and found it yielded the best results when the margin was large and poorly performed when it was small. We hypothesize our method's limitations in handling small margins might be due to its sensitivity to noise, suggesting further research is needed to overcome this issue. Research into how speech is perceived has often focused on natural speech from male and female speakers, overlooking synthetic speech from text-to-speech systems. Our study fills this gap by examining how listeners evaluate virtual job applicants through speech, including how specific voice characteristics are received. We discovered that combining different voice attributes, especially those related to speech clarity and emotional expression, impacts listeners' perceptions. Specifically, blending certain rough voice qualities can create a more capable image, whereas combining tense or strained voices is seen as counterproductive. Moreover, listeners' evaluations are influenced by how well a synthetic voice sounds natural, with more natural-sounding voices being preferred over less natural ones, even if their speech is less clear. Ultimately, listeners' choices between synthetic and real voices depend on factors such as voice quality and emotional expression, with more natural-sounding synthetic voices preferred over less natural ones, even if their speech is less clear. Our findings have implications for the design of text-to-speech systems and how listeners evaluate speakers based on their voice quality. Our research highlights the significance of voice design in text-to-speech systems and suggests that developers could create more convincing synthetic speakers by considering a broader range of speech characteristics. Our study also contributes to a better understanding of how listeners make decisions when evaluating speakers, including real and synthetic voices. Our method, which simulates a virtual job interview, provides a useful tool for researchers and practitioners to gain insights into listeners' decisions. Our research has potential to inform practitioners how to train human evaluators, including strategies for combining real and synthetic speech data. Our research can be replicated by interested researchers, including by using the same voice samples and evaluation methods. Our research includes a repository with the experiment's code and data, located at https://github.com/andreagemelli/speech-perception. Among the various approaches to change detection, unsupervised methods are particularly valuable in settings where labeling data is impractical or the scenarios under study are yet to be encountered during training. A notable example is the iterative self-supervised model, self-supervised multi-temporal (SMT), which converts change detection into a self-supervised anomaly detection problem. By employing three distinct self-supervised strategies to create training data, SMT can learn its parameters without prior labeling. Furthermore, by training and evaluating models under different configurations while adjusting the proportion of older images, we gain insights into the model's performance across various contexts. Despite this potential's inherent anharmonicity, the fluid's temperature and density properties can be scaled in accordance with the principle of corresponding states.  To verify this, the fluid's viscosity was mapped across various conditions, and the results showed that only density scaling is sufficient to establish a universal viscosity map.  To further clarify, the fluid's real-space interactions were analyzed, revealing the presence of "fountain flow".  Fountain flow's characteristic flow rate was determined as a function of the fluid's shear rate and density, thereby establishing a universal flow map.  Furthermore, the fluid's real-space data were used to derive an approximation of its shear correlation function, whose time evolution can be modeled using the Bessel function.  By combining these elements, the fluid's viscosity and correlation function were incorporated into a universal flow map, thereby allowing the development of a universal fluid dynamic model that applies across the conditions examined.  Notably, the model's predictions showed a notable discrepancy of just 15% compared to experimental data on the fluids carbon dioxide and methane.  Ultimately, the model's limitations stem from the failure to accurately capture the behavior of associated molecular fluids, thereby leaving room for further theoretical exploration. Artificial intelligence has become an integral part of our daily lives, with machine learning models such as Deep Neural Networks increasingly relying on compute capacity and memory. However, many advanced ML models exceed the capabilities of standard desktop computers, necessitating specialized hardware like GPUs, FPUs, and vast amounts of memory. A promising trend aims to deploy these powerful models on consumer devices, despite their limited resources, for applications like speech recognition in smart speakers and gesture detection in wearables. Unfortunately, current ML models often require massive memory and processing power, making them impractical for these devices. This study presents a novel, lightweight neural network design aimed at improving AI capabilities on resource-constrained devices. By adopting novel, innovative techniques, this architecture achieves state-of-the-art performance while significantly reducing memory and computation demands. Furthermore, a high-performance, custom accelerator is proposed to accelerate the deployment of these models on device limitations. Two prototype SoCs were developed, featuring hardware implementation that outperformed software-based approaches. Custom accelerators achieved a power efficiency factor of 3.38 and showcased the benefits of hardware acceleration for on-edge ML applications. Comparative analysis with other ML models revealed that our approach delivered the best balance of accuracy, computation, and memory requirements. A open-source ML framework named M$^3$ was also developed, enabling the implementation of ML models with variable precision (fixed-point arithmetic) and providing fixed-point conversion tools for the conversion of standard ML models into fixed-point formats suitable for the custom accelerator. This framework has been successfully applied to the conversion of ResNet-20, YOLOv3, and U-Net models, among others, and provides support for the custom accelerator through a dynamic, hardware-based scheduling mechanism. To tackle the variety of real-time demands in practical embedded systems, the T-Visordynamic scheduling engine was designed to accommodate multiple polynomial-based real-time formulas. Initially developed for Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling applications with single real-time formula requirements, the T-Visor has been expanded to cater to complex scenarios. This enhancement preserves its initial low overhead, which was initially around 1.2 kilobytes and 10 microcodes. To facilitate complex scenarios, the T-Visor integrates multiple task groups, each with their own polynomial-based real-time formula. This partitioning can be automatically optimized utilizing dynamic task placement algorithms, which minimize the maximum task group utilization while considering the available processing idle periods. To achieve this, the maximum possible group loading is determined by iteratively increasing the task loading within each group, which is validated through simple yet efficient algorithms that keep memory access at a minimum. This process maximizes the overall system throughput while maintaining low overhead, which is less prone to performance degradation caused by system complexity. To validate the proposed method, the maximum achievable group loading was measured along with the resulting system throughput improvements, which were shown to be effectively capped at 100 percent in both cases and boosted by four times in throughput, respectively, with different task distributions. Moreover, the overhead of this partitioning approach remained under 6 percent, which is deemed acceptable in most real-world applications. This research was published in the Journal of Real-Time Systems under the title "Exploiting Real-Time Formulas Heterogeneity in DVFS-Based Systems: A Low-Overhead Scheduling Approach."  Further, the scalability of this partitioning approach has been demonstrated using up to 16 different task formulas, which is verified through an acknowledgement from the REM-RISCsys research network. Additionally, the dynamic sampling rate-based scheduling method was successfully integrated into the T-Visor. This integration allows for dynamic task grouping according to their sampling rates. To achieve this, the dynamic sampling rate-based scheduling method was tested and verified. This research was presented at the 24th Euromicro Conference for Real-Time Systems, which was hosted in Pisa, Italy.
