This research introduces a novel, optimized implementation of the Fast Multipole Method (FMM), which efficiently handles irregularly-shaped data arrays to calculate gravitational interactions between objects. In contrast to existing FMM implementations that assume uniform data grids, our algorithm generates an adaptive sparse matrix that reduces computations by eliminating unnecessary calculations. Furthermore, our implementation of the FMM algorithm is designed to integrate seamlessly with the Healpix framework, widely used in astrophysical maps, and has been successfully applied to various celestial and theoretical scenarios. This includes simulations of cosmic microwave background observations, galaxy surveys, and theoretical models of space-based observatories. This paper outlines the underlying technical considerations and presents benchmark analysis demonstrating the speed advantages of our adaptive FMM implementation. This research is expected to facilitate the integration of the FMM algorithm into healpix-based astrophysical simulations, facilitating seamless computations of gravitational interactions between objects. Additional software implementations are also available for inquiry.

This study focuses on upgrading a conventional spin maser system, known for its strong radio interference avoidance properties, by integrating digital signal processing. This upgraded system, powered by a digital oscillator, can change its resonant frequency in very short periods of time. As a result, the radio noise it produces becomes difficult to predict and takes on a characteristic similar to white Gaussian noise. Consequently, the effectiveness of the radio interference avoidance properties, which were previously assessed in relation to deterministic noise patterns, are severely diminished when digital signal processing is not utilized. This processor utilizes a bank of pre-calculated sine wave samples, synthesized with a digital oscillator, whose frequency is set using an efficient phase-locked loop system. This phase-locked loop system is controlled by a specialized algorithm that can change the maser's resonant frequency in very short periods, while also minimizing the associated sine wave frequency errors. The proposed digital processor also switches between different pre-synthesized sine wave frequencies stored in an lookup table, allowing the maser to produce a spectrum with specific patterns and reduced noise. The algorithm used in the phase-locked loop system is then analyzed using various methods, such as maximum likelihood estimation, to assess its efficiency. This study demonstrates that by leveraging the phase-locked loop's frequency acquisition capabilities, it is possible to estimate the parameters of a spin system, previously used for radio interference avoidance, in the presence of digital signal processing. Multi-Lingual Scene Text Detection and Recognition (MSCTR) has been gaining significant interest in recent years, and a major challenge has been dealing with out-of-vocabulary words, which typically don't get recognized by standard models. In this study, we introduce a novel word challenge dataset, named OutOfVoc20, containing a multi-lingual collection of 2000+ out-of-vocabulary words for 20 languages, which was previously missing from MSCTR datasets. To show the potential of MSCTR models in tackling this challenge, we employ transfer learning by training these models on the new OOV dataset, and our findings indicate that they can successfully learn to recognize the out-of-vocabulary words by leveraging contextual information from surrounding words. Building on this research, we propose an intuitive representation that combines the word's appearance, semantic, and contextual information using OOV-induced mixed-task learning, and show that this approach significantly improves the OOV recognition performance. The findings from the OOV-induced mixed-task learning framework suggest that MSCTR models can effectively generalize to unfamiliar words by identifying common word patterns and categorizing them into recognizable groups. The proposed framework and OOV dataset are now publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/ali-101/ooov20-data. We aim to believe that releasing these resources will accelerate the MSCTR field in addressing the OOV challenge. The research findings are presented in this ArXiv paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.02630. The top MSCTR models that achieved the best performance on the OOV dataset were ultimately selected as prize-winners in the 2021-2022 ICAR-CV OOV Challenge competition. The proposed approach significantly outperformed the current best practices in MSCTR by achieving an OOV recognition performance gain of +81.9% and +77.2% for the Word-Upper-Lower and Word-Upper-only representation schemes, respectively, when the model was trained using the new OOV-induced mixed-task learning framework. Notably, we've discovered a distinct set of massless fields specific to each two-dimensional anti de-Sitter fixed point, stemming from the decoupling process. X-ray diffraction experiments conducted on ammonium sulfate single crystals revealed an increase in entropy through enthalpy exchange during its 228 K phase transition. However, two previous studies failed to identify the origin of this entropy gain, attributing only a small portion to disorder resulting from ammonium ion displacement. We argue that this previous claim is erroneous and instead propose that the observed entropy increase is primarily a consequence of lattice inflation resulting from increased bond covalency between sulfate and ammonium ions. We support our argument with lattice inflation simulations and an accompanying discussion on its significance. Furthermore, we suggest that this phenomenon may be common among other polar compounds exhibiting large entropy variations. Finally, we present an alternative that could facilitate the direct observation of this entropy source: using terahertz spectroscopy to measure the thermal expansion of these compounds. We verified this approach by analyzing THz data on hydrochloride and finding that ammonium compounds are suitable candidates for this type of investigation. We also outline a potential route for employing room-temperature THz spectroscopy as a means of evaluating pharmaceuticals' stability via their thermal expansion characteristics. We identified a correlation between THz optical conductivity and compound stability: compounds with higher and more temperature-dependent THz conductivity tend to be less stable. Given that THz technology is already being used to analyze pharmaceuticals, it is now feasible to employ this method to predict their stability based on their thermal expansion properties. We suggest design strategies for stabilizing these compounds by intentionally decreasing their THz conductivity. Consequently, this approach could be applied to other materials. We also outline a potential route for developing stable, customized pharmaceutical forms with regulated THz properties. We attribute this phenomenon to the clathrate's ability to regulate its THz properties and the stability of its components. The concept of probability-matching has historically been associated with risk-averse and risk-prone behaviors, particularly those learned through trial and error. Contrary to expectations, recent studies have found that probability-matching doesn't necessarily imply cognitive biases towards caution or recklessness. Instead, this tendency may indicate how learned agents integrate negative experiences to adjust their behavior. We've discovered in a finite Markov decision process that probability-matching can be viewed as a form of "memory-integration," where an agent's optimal policy may effectively combine new and past information. This finding is grounded in the idea that agents can manifest two contrasting attitudes towards loss, characterized by avoidance or seeking out dangerous situations, without being inherently cautious or daring. Our analysis, relying on a state-space visitation frequency metric, suggests that probability-matching is closely linked to two strategies that simultaneously mitigate loss and minimize memory usage. To explore the nature of these strategies, we've employed a graph-theoretic framework, highlighting situations in which these approaches can be considered optimal. The analysis points out that all our findings are quantitatively validated using reinforcement learning algorithms, including Q-learning and policy iteration. The work offers insights into how learned behaviors might appear as a form of probability-matching without being driven by cognitive biases towards risk aversion or recklessness. Moreover, it identifies specific situations in which these biases can emerge as complementary motives for adapting to new environments. Ultimately, it suggests that probability-matching can serve as an indicator of optimal policy learning that incorporates past experiences in a balanced manner. The research also raises important implications for sampling methods, such as importance sampling, suggesting that probability-matching can result from overemphasizing rare, high-reward outcomes. The study concludes by highlighting a fundamental paradox: while probability-matching can be an efficient indicator of optimal learning strategies, it may also represent contrasting attitudes towards loss that are contradictory with each other. The advancement of quantum computing has sparked a renewed interest in quantum Bayes, an application of Bayesian methods in quantum computer programming. The process of Bayesian unfolding is a suitable candidate for measurement error mitigation and has been adapted for use on quantum computers. The conventional Bayesian unfolding approach, however, experiences a significant increase in computational complexity with the rise in event count data. This limitation can be overcome through the employment of iterative Bayesian unfolding. In this research, the iterative Bayesian unfolding technique was successfully implemented on a noisy quantum simulator. The project demonstrated the process of Bayesian unfolding and assessed its performance using a histogram representing peak widths from Simulated IDQuantum's Qaa-1 devices. The results indicate that the iterative Bayesian unfolding approach yields a substantial improvement in computational efficiency by a factor of 846 when processing 100,000 data events compared to the conventional method. The research further highlights the potential of quantum computers to accelerate Bayesian unfolding, thereby making the measurement process approximately 84 times faster. The study also shows that the conventional and iterative methods yield equivalent results, thus suggesting that the iterative Bayesian unfolding approach can be used to mitigate measurement errors on quantum computers without a substantial penalty in terms of accuracy. The research further indicates that the measurement process can be further enhanced by leveraging multi-qubit entanglement, an invaluable resource in quantum computing. The potential of combining the iterative Bayesian unfolding with ANNEAL's use case may also be explored in further research, an approach that yields optimal results but requires careful tuning to achieve the optimal correlation between posterior and prior distributions. The research was carried out using open-source Python code that is compatible with the project's GitHub repository, thus allowing the code to be shared freely with the scientific community. The research further includes Simulated IDQuantum's Qaa-1 devices' error profiles that can be utilized for measurement error mitigation processes. The research further indicates that the Qaa-1 devices' error profiles can be modeled using a mixture of two Gaussian distributions, thus providing an adequate fit for the error data. The research further suggests that the occurrence of occasional much higher error values may be attributed to physical defects in the quantum hardware. The research further provides an insight into the potential applications of quantum Bayes in terms of measurement error mitigation, a critical aspect of quantum computing, an area that is highly unlikely to be replaced by classical methods. The research further concludes by stating that the fusion of quantum computing and Bayesian data analysis has just begun to unlock numerous possibilities, an area that is highly likely to exhibit significant advancements in the future. When interacting with an unfamiliar system, users' understanding of how their inputs affect the system can greatly impact their ability to accomplish tasks efficiently. Previous studies on robotic systems reveal that these agents can improve user performance by making their task parameters, such as temperatures in a coffee machine, visible. However, there is limited knowledge on how a robot agent facilitates human-robot collaboration when interacting with a task that involves a complex sequence of actions. In this study, we investigate the effects of a robot agent's behavior on human performance in a pick-and-place task using the UR5 robot arm. We discovered that revealing the robot's chosen object mappings, either for picking-up or placement tasks, increases the human's accuracy. Furthermore, we found that making the robot's mappings visible for both tasks enhances human performance overall. We also discovered that humans tend to trust the robot's mappings in a predictable manner, such as through sequential tasks, and that this trust has a positive effect on efficiency. Ultimately, we recommend designers of collaborative robotic systems that execute sequential tasks for human-robot collaboration to design agents that can reveal their internal workings to achieve optimal collaboration results. High-resolution CT imaging is crucial in advanced industrial applications, but its effectiveness can be hindered by hardware failures and external disruptions, resulting in noisy and incomplete data. To restore original images from degraded CT scans, we introduce a novel 3D attention-based deep learning framework, utilizing knowledge from multiple energy measurements and adaptive weighting. The model consists of two core components: (1) a double residual network that leverages multi-energy data to capture features in sparse and dense domains; (2) a multi-scale attention mechanism that prioritizes relevant data in both spatial and frequency spaces, enhancing the reconstruction process. Through extensive simulations and real-world experiments, our proposed method demonstrates significant improvements in image quality and reconstruction accuracy when processing data with various types of noise, noise patches, and sparse underexposed data compared to traditional CT reconstruction techniques. The model's source code is available on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/jhtiesbu/3D-Attention-CT-Recon. The research is supported by the National Science Foundation Grant No. 2153661. The proposed method's potential impact is further validated by its high potential for application in medical and industrial imaging scenarios. The anticipated benefits and limitations of this method are summarized in a dedicated section at the end of this article. Furthermore, this article provides a concrete example of a special section, namely 'Systematic Approach', with an aim to promote a meaningful and systematic approach to research, particularly in areas with existing widespread applications and a significant potential for application, in this case CT technology. The intended audience of this article consists of researchers and practitioners familiar with deep learning, as well as a broader audience interested in related fields. The proposal is open to feedback from other specialized communities, such as industrial and biomedical imaging experts. This paper introduces an effective gap width concept that facilitates the simulation of light transmission through resonant cavities found in phononic crystals composed of flat surfaces. The method involves replacing the complex grooves with a simplified emergent gap and recalculating the associated effective parameters. When incorporated into a beam propagation model, this effective gap width approach yields highly accurate predictions of light transmission. In comparison to local models, the findings show that the phononic crystal's high transmission capabilities can be more precisely estimated using the effective gap width concept. Contextual named entity retrieval (CONSER) is an advanced application of named entity retrieval that identifies entities from unstructured text given a specific context. For instance, it can locate a specific person's mentions in a document, given their name as the context. Typically, CONSERS utilize machine-readable texts and provide annotations manually. To address this issue, we focus on applying advances in neural architecture search and efficiently training fast CONSERS. We develop a high-performance CONSER through continuous iteration of structure search and optimization of performance minimization. The results show a significant improvement in search time from days to hours and performance from 83.2% to 84.4% with our proposed model. Furthermore, we release our project as an open-source framework to facilitate research in this field. The repository can be accessed at: https://github.com/ai4pros/ANECONS. This research is an extension of our previously published studies, repackaging and enhancing the original codebase with new findings. Specifically, we integrate structure search into the training process, reducing search time drastically, as well as enhance the model's performance using knowledge distillation. We provide detailed information on the model's design, the search process, and the dataset used. Additionally, we present the effectiveness of our model in several entity-type specific datasets. We aim to make significant contributions to the field of CONSERS by resolving the complex problem of efficiently training fast and high-performance models. This study offers solutions to the challenges associated with searching for structures in large-spaces with complex criteria and high computational costs. Currently available visualization tools can show connections between individual observations (points) and their related characteristics (bar charts, scatter plots), yet there is a lack of support for linking observations with aggregated or summary-based displays (such as histograms, heatmaps, and parallel sets). We propose a new approach that extends linking mechanisms to these types of displays, enabling users to navigate between focused observations and broader contextual information displayed on the screen at the same time. In addition, users can set filters directly within these contextual displays to expand the scope further. Inspired by the architecture of the ggplot2 graphics system, we have developed a system to derive contextual displays with built-in linking capabilities, or "temporal plots". We have modified ggplot2 functions to create these plots, allowing users to view data at different levels of detail, such as observing individual cases and understanding how they distribute across broader categories at the same time. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by incorporating it into Tableau's visualization platform and conducting user studies, which reveal that participants highly value the links with summary statistics and contextual information displays. Annotated demonstrations illustrate various applications of this technique and showcase its potential in supporting iterative data analysis processes. We discuss challenges and limitations, including the difficulty in deciding which level of detail is most relevant and the issue of data duplication. Finally, future areas of exploration are identified, such as leveraging geographical data to enhance connections between observations and their contextual information. Overall, our contribution establishes a framework for extending established visualization linking methods to more complex types of data displays, enabling users to navigate complex data sets. By developing a systematic approach, we have shown that this technique can be applied to data analysis platforms to facilitate deeper understanding of complex data. As the field continues to evolve, we anticipate a significant impact from this research in supporting data analysis and scientific investigation. Real-world issues are often tackled using more complex models than is necessary. Homophily and heterogeneity in Electronic Health Records (EHRs) complicate the performance of graph neural networks (GNNs), resulting in inconsistent outcomes when trained on the integrated patient graph. To mitigate these issues, research proposes adjusting the GNN's attention to balance global and local patterns. However, this approach relies on non-linear, differentiable functions and therefore cannot be applied to non-differentiable GNNs, such as graph convolutional neural networks (GCN). To overcome this limitation, the method depicted damped stochastic gradient descent with layer-specific momentum and weight decay. Experimental findings on simulated data and the open-source MIMIC-III dataset demonstrate the significantly improved robustness of GCNs when using this adjusted approach. Consequently, the method can enhance the performance of GNNs on diverse real-world datasets. The source code is available at https://github.com/quantifyingweather/robust-gnn.git. This research has been accepted for presentation at the 33rd Annual ACM Conference on Knowledge Discovery. 

Note: The approach discussed in the thesis is designed for node-level classification and therefore, when applied to link prediction tasks, results in an increased area under the curve (AUC) by a factor of 20. For classification tasks, the method leads to an improved F1-score of up to one percentage point. To mitigate heterogeneity and homophily in EHRs, the approach has been successfully applied to non-linear GNNs, such as GCNs and PoolNet, as well as GNNs with non-differentiable attention, such as AttentionNet.

Our model, Software BERT, is a unique adaptation of the BERT model designed to capture software-specific word relationships by incorporating contextual features within the software development lifecycle. By fine-tuning BERT on datasets from the Software Dataset Repository, our model achieved impressive results, outperforming competing models like fastText and ELMo on various requirement-related tasks. In comparison to the standard BERT model, our revised version, ECL BERT, demonstrated improved task performance, utilizing a distinct dataset specifically tailored for the software development field. Moreover, our model's parameter analysis revealed that the distribution of unique non-project specific words, used to initialize the BERT model, significantly impacted its performance, highlighting potential areas for further research in the future. Ultimately, our model, Software BERT, serves as a valuable resource for the software engineering community by offering a trained BERT model, along with its unique pre-training data, to enhance the understanding of cross-project features with minimal context changes. The model, our code, and relevant dataset are publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ziyi-li/Software_BERT. This research was partially supported by NSF grant RUI-1914484.

This research addresses the problem of minimizing total network energy consumption in a cooperative communication system, which allocates power and schedules relays for multiple users with varying data rates. A reduced complexity solution is developed, incorporating an alternating optimization algorithm consisting of sub-problems solved by the Dinkelbach method and the water-filling algorithm. The result is a minimized overall network energy consumption at each transmission time slot. Simulations reveal that the proposed solution consumes less energy than other options, particularly those not accounting for relay scheduling. It also meets the data rate requirements of all users and converges quickly to an optimal solution. Compared to other schemes, the reduced complexity solution yields significant reductions in energy consumption, particularly those not initially scheduling relays according to data rates. Furthermore, its performance approaches the optimal energy consumption determined by a computationally intensive, two-stage optimization method. In addition to energy consumption, this paper explores the impact of the proposed solution on other key performance indicators, such as end-user data rates and channel utilization. This research introduces a novel approach for aligning downsampled LIDAR point clouds over time, incorporating a dynamic filtering mechanism to segregate static from dynamic components within the scene. A proposed boundary point detection method effectively pinpoints areas where movement has occurred. A dynamic filter is employed to eliminate static points, resulting in a global overlap of remaining points, thus facilitating registration. To refine the overall registration process, local overlaps are identified through an analysis of the point-to-grid local feature match, supplemented by a proposed optimization method. Evaluation of the proposed approach leverages KITTI dataset, showcasing its superiority over conventional global overlap-based registration methods, particularly in urban environments with both static and dynamic features. Notably, downsampled point clouds with fewer than 10,000 points can be efficiently aligned using the proposed technique. A comparative analysis against traditional methods, including iterative closest point and hierarchical net, reveals a minimum 1.5 times increase in processing speed and up to a 2.2 point improvement in registration accuracy. The source code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/AgHacker/PCSam. Moreover, a containerized version of the code is provided on https://docker.aghacker.com/. Construction of a synthetic 3D model using the aligned point clouds, represented as a mesh, is also possible with the proposed approach. The resulting 3D model can be visualized using the meshlab containerized version, accessible through a web interface at https://3d.aghacker.com/. A tutorial illustrating the model reconstruction process is available on YouTube at https://youtube.aghacker.com/. Furthermore, a mesh file obtained through this process is provided for evaluation upon request. The proposed method has been validated using the KITTI dataset, yielding a reconstruction accuracy of less than 0.05 meters. Satellite images are essential data for numerous satellite-based applications, but their vast quantity and relatively slow acquisition rate make them vulnerable to data contamination and imbalance. This inherent imbalance impacts machine learning techniques used for satellite image analysis, where the classes with fewer instances typically require more resources for resampling or reorganization to achieve a balance. On the other end, deep learning methods have successfully addressed the problem, but their complexity and rigidity limit their adaptability to diverse scenarios. In response, we present a two-part framework that first identifies and rematches data patterns for imbalance correction. Secondly, a transfer learning approach is used to leverage features from imbalanced datasets. We evaluate and validate the effectiveness of our proposed framework with real-world datasets from plant disease detection and renewable energy applications. The framework's code will be made available through an open-source repository on the GitHub platform with the URL specified. Furthermore, a detailed description of the framework's implementation, including its source code, will be provided in the paper. With the aim of promoting reproducibility, our proposed framework's efficacy will be demonstrated using notable benchmarks, with specific emphasis on datasets that are commonly used in remote sensing research, including the dataset for detecting planthopper and yellowing leaves, which causes damage to coconut palms, and the dataset for binary overlap classification, among others. This study demonstrates the efficacy of subject-based data resampling and transfer learning from related tasks to improve the performance of machine learning techniques used for satellite image analysis, showcasing significant improvement in classification metrics such as overall accuracy, especially for the detection of scarce instances in the data pool. With the transfer learning approach, our proposed framework further enhances the overall accuracy by a margin of 2% and also increases the forerunning F1 score for the minority class by 3%. In addition, the proposed subject-based data resampling and transfer learning approaches have been successfully tested and validated on imbalanced data from diverse real-world applications, including plant disease detection, renewable energy analysis, and other remote sensing research datasets, indicating their potential for widespread use. Moreover, the proposed framework's performance is shown to be superior to that of conventional methods used in data resampling and learning, with specific improvements of around 6% and 9% in overall accuracy and F1 score for the minority class, respectively. In addition to remote sensing research, the proposed framework has also been tested on diverse practical scenarios, including data analysis for building extraction, and has been found to outperform state-of-the-art methods used for energy efficiency and classification metrics. The role of electron dynamics and non-linear light interaction in metallic materials is investigated using ultrafast spectroscopy and density functional theory. Upon high-fluence irradiation of metallic nickel, non-linear changes in absorption parallel those of third-order non-linear susceptibility, driven by electron redistribution. The observed electron dynamics aligns with the two-temperature model, yet subsequent energy dissipation occurs at a slower rate than typically expected. Utilizing DFT, computational models based on both the two-temperature and three-temperature scales for electron and lattice thermalization have been created to simulate the laser-matter interaction process. The results demonstrate that a model considering electron shell contributions more accurately predicts the measured decay rate of lattice heat than the standard two-temperature model. Furthermore, computational results show that lattice thermalization via elastic collisions is the primary mechanism for the observed slow dissipation rate in the system. The simulation also reveals that changes in electronic structure and magnetic ordering of nickel can occur within the material's electron relaxation period. The theoretical framework developed in this work provides a valuable tool for understanding and interpreting ultrafast laser-matter interaction experiments across various systems. The experimental findings and computational results have significant implications for the design and optimization of plasmonic enhanced coherent electron-phonon processes and other applications where extended electron relaxation times are beneficial. The influence of structural changes and magnetic ordering on the coherent and incoherent electron-phonon processes is currently under investigation. The study of electronic and structural changes during laser-matter interaction may provide a means to manipulate and optimize the temporary changes in magnetic ordering, as observed in this work. The experimental observation of changes in magnetic ordering in nickel was verified using time-resolved magneto-optical spectroscopy, as detailed in the supporting information. Adversarial attacks on Deep Neural Network-based systems have significant real-world implications. In the field of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), research has primarily been confined to understanding their theoretical underpinnings. There has been a lack of in-depth exploration into the adversarial resistance capabilities of GANs. This research delves into GANs' robustness under various adversarial attacks and compares different architectures in terms of their ability to withstand such threats. Through our investigation using the MNIST dataset, we assess the resilience of both non-adversarial and adversarial-robust GANs. This study helps establish a baseline reference point for designing secure GANs and contributes to advancing the knowledge in this area by presenting innovative architectures that can mitigate adversarial attacks. The findings from this research are made publicly accessible through a repository on GitHub, including the implementation of architectures and adversarial attack codes. Additionally, the research outcomes have been presented in detail through a visualized dashboard. Furthermore, the source code and trained model outputs are available for reproduction and future reference. This research also facilitates the development of a comparative framework for evaluating GAN architectures in terms of their robustness against adversarial attacks. The comparison is performed using metrics such as Frechet Inception Distance (FID) and adversarial attack success rates. To facilitate reproibility, the research reports all the relevant metrics and architectural design choices employed. This study aims to facilitate the design of secure GANs by contributing to both the research community and the broader public through open-source repositories and open research practices. The proposed framework and architectures have potential applications in various real-world domains such as surveillance, power grid management, and autonomous vehicles to name a few, where implementation of robust GANs can provide added security against potential threats. To address the challenge of annotating data from multiple hospitals, we employ a novel approach which first identifies known lesion locations in unlabeled data through crowdsourcing, then utilizes these references for training a convolutional neural network to segment lesions. We discover that experience replay, which re-trains our model using previously successful predictions, significantly enhances its performance. We also find that using augmented images generated by transforming ground truth data is an effective method for increasing our model's robustness. These techniques, combined with the use of domain confusion, ultimately yield results that rival state-of-the-art performance and demonstrate the effectiveness of crowd-sourcing and experience replay for mitigating the limitations associated with dataset size and diversity. With a global mean segmentation error of 4.98 mm, our model secured 4th place in the competition. This leads to the question of whether this enhanced comparison is connected to the continuity of optimal transport. The answer is yes, and this equivalence holds under relatively mild conditions. When the source and target measures are the same, we've developed a simplified and more stable method for solving the problem. This new approach involves sampling from a discrete space and using a comparison metric that is sensitive to data points, and it is proven to converge to the original problem. When applied to various data sets, our method beats traditional methods in giving a more accurate linear representation of the data. This new framework also allows us to measure how continuous or discrete a data set is by comparing its optimal transport distances with respect to different base measures, and through testing, we found that each data set has its own unique characteristics. Furthermore, using this metric, we classified unbalanced data and identified the most representative information it contains. We explore the potential of hybrid models that blend data-driven and domain-inspired approaches, using neural networks to represent unknown components and symbolic expressions for incorporated domain knowledge. Our results on several mathematical problems indicate that these hybrid models yield superior performance compared to purely data-based models, particularly when the domain knowledge is accurate and the neural network's uncertainty about its parameters is minimized. Furthermore, we find that incorporating domain knowledge enables hybrid models to perform well even with less extensive training on relevant mathematical expressions, making them a valuable option for scenarios where access to large datasets is restricted. Ultimately, we anticipate that hybrid models will assume a more prominent role in mathematical problem-solving tasks, with ongoing research likely to lead to more effective integration of symbolic and neural computing paradigms. The spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet RbCo2YZ14 is characterized by weakly interacting Y3+ ions and strongly interacting Co2+ ions with strong anisotropy. By incorporating pressure, researchers have uncovered a phase diagram containing an unstable normal spin liquid and two polar crystalline phases with unique properties. At a density higher than 1000 kg/m^3, the spin-liquid region gives way to two polar phases: a orthorhombic structure involving a high-anisotropy component and a uniaxial ferroelectric component, and a monoclinic structure involving a high-anisotropy component. At a density higher than 1300 kg/m^3, the upper phase transition gives way to a monoclinic structure involving a low-anisotropy component. Unusual properties of these polar phases are evident in heat capacity measurements that exhibit a drop to zero: for the orthorhombic structure, this occurs at low temperatures, while for the monoclinic structure, this occurs at an even lower temperature. Moreover, the monoclinic structure exhibits a strong anomaly at the upper phase transition temperature. These results are consistent with theoretical predictions of unstable normal spin-liquid and polar normal spin liquids at a density higher than 1000 kg/m^3. Excitingly, the unusual properties of these polar phases have been identified for the first time in a quantum spin system. Recent studies have demonstrated that pretrained language models can efficiently process any language, but they still rely on specific tokens and word combinations that inevitably appear during training. This limitation leads to perceived performance issues when these models are applied to unseen domains, largely caused by the role of special tokens. To address this concern, we propose a novel approach that isolates special tokens from natural text, creating a separate dataset for these tokens and retraining the model to improve its resilience to spam input and maintain consistency with its trained behavior. Experimental results on the GLUE benchmark show that our method achieves a significant improvement, with models trained on the isolated special token dataset outperforming those trained on combined datasets. Moreover, our approach yields better outcomes compared to models trained in a seen spam environment, proving the effectiveness of our method in managing special tokens and maintaining model consistency. This study offers recommendations for handling special tokens within pretrained language models and provides an open-source implementation for easy replication. The research paper can be found at arXiv:2206.12491. The project's source code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/davidcun/IsolatingSpecialTokens. To facilitate model experimentation, an adapted version of ALBERT-xlarge is hosted at https://huggingface.co/dcun/ALBERT_xlarge_isp_tokenized/ST_stateless. To preserve the integrity of the pre-trained language models, this work chooses not to release the original datasets that include special tokens. The problem of measuring a system's improvements has significant implications within network mathematics, encompassing various applications such as identifying the optimal route and discovering community structures. A renowned assessment metric is the normalized covariance, which indicates the degree to which a system's modifications align with expectations. Although generalized degree-based metrics are more widely employed, research has demonstrated that normalized covariance yields better outcomes in the case of adding nodes to existing networks. A novel approach for system evaluation has been introduced, combining the benefits of both generalized degree-based and covariance metrics. Through comprehensive analysis, it is shown that this new method excels in detecting genuine improvements in random as well as real-world network systems, outperforming the established benchmark metrics in this regard. Furthermore, this novel approach enables accurate measurement of the effective sensitivity of systems characterized by random walk or disease spread dynamics, where it outperforms competing metrics. As such, this new method has promising implications for the accurate detection of realistic system improvements based on network structure evolution. The study's findings are made available through open-source software.

Recent advancements in transformer-based models for supersedural NLI have not fully
considered the impact of semantic negation, a crucial factor in NLI. To address
this, we propose the Negation-Informed NLI (NINLI) dataset, consisting of NLI
samples modified to incorporate semantic negation from human curators. The
dataset is aligned with two levels of negation, affecting NLI performance by 6.4%
when using a state-of-the-art transformer model. To help NLI models generalize
better, we also release BINE, a binary classification benchmark incorporating
the NINLI dataset. Moreover, we propose a method to automatically detect negation
in NLI data, identifying 35.9% of human-written hypotheses as containing
semantic negation from human curators. The NINLI dataset and other resources
are available at https://github.com/AIforNLP/NINLI. This research is supported
by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (No. 62176202).

This research develops a new method to efficiently determine the price of Asian options with early exercise advantages, options that have been challenging due to their nature. We employ single Laplace transforms to derive exact solutions for options with geometric, arithmetic, and general series-style cashflows, achieving complete accuracy. Our method combines the advantages of exact transformation methods and the computational efficiency of Laplace transforms, extending the applicability of this technique to a broader range of scenarios. We provide a comprehensive framework that allows the derived Laplace transforms to be used for approximate option pricing as time approaches zero and verify the accuracy of this approximation through numerical self-validation. Furthermore, we utilize the obtained Laplace transforms in convolutionless exponential time difference (ETD) schemes and standard finite difference methods to explore the properties of the option in a time-dependent environment. We also explore the pricing of dividend-paying stocks with periodic dividend payouts, findings that support approximating a periodic dividend yield in such scenarios. Lastly, we demonstrate the practical application of this method to scenario-based stochastic pricing and compare the results to well-established approaches in the field. Our study supplements the existing literature on exact transformation methods, providing valuable insights and contributing to a deeper understanding of option pricing. The key to bridging this gap lies in understanding the similar structures shared between one-dimensional and two-dimensional cuprates, allowing for the utilization of a single theoretical framework to study and describe the evolution of properties and phenomena across the cuprate family. In this study, a theoretical model based on the concept of spinons is developed to investigate the properties of 1D and 2D cuprates, focusing on their dependence on doping levels. The model employs a unique adjustable parameter, representing the coupling between spinons and electrons, which enables accurate simulation of the characteristics of cuprate superconductors across different doping levels, including their resistance, magnetic susceptibility, superconducting properties, and energy spectra, all while maintaining consistency within a controlled theoretical framework. Furthermore, this model predicts a critical point near 10% doping where the behavior of 2D cuprates changes significantly, potentially corresponding to the onset of an effective 1D state. By comparing the anisotropy of superconducting gaps, we demonstrate that 1D cuprates exhibit significantly stronger confinement than 2D cuprates, strongly supporting the existence of an effective 1D system within 2D cuprates. Finally, this model offers an in-depth understanding of high-temperature superconductivity in cuprates, revealing its underlying one-dimensional nature and providing a theoretical explanation for the observed effects of impurities, the curvature of doping-dependent properties, and the limitations of Drachman's approximation in the context of superconductivity. By establishing a direct connection between cuprate superconductivity, antiferromagnetism, and confinement through spinon physics, we have successfully integrated the knowledge gained from research on 1D and 2D cuprates within a unified theoretical framework. As a result, we have identified several critical areas for further experimental verification, including testing for effects of impurities on spinon confinement, examining anisotropy in superconducting systems, and finding evidence for spinon confinement in highly doped cuprates. Moreover, we have proposed novel methods for measuring spinon physics, such as using highly energetic particle scattering and measuring energy spectra at very low energies. Understanding access to healthcare facilities, such as those providing HIV treatment, is crucial for evaluating equity in patient treatment opportunities. Using smartphone GPS data, this study examined access to HIV care facilities in South Africa and analyzed factors influencing treatment likelihood. The results showed that familiarity with travel times to HIV care facilities did not significantly impact treatment likelihood, suggesting that other factors such as social relationships and individual characteristics like income and marital status play a more pivotal role. The research also demonstrated that HIV treatment sites consistently underestimate travel times, typically by more than double, implying a need for better planning of facility distributions and investment in programs aimed at improving access to these services. To address this issue, this study proposes the use of geographical buffering techniques to evaluate access and identify optimal locations for new HIV care facilities through the evaluation of different placement scenarios. The integration of sampling methods is also recommended to enhance the efficiency of these evaluations. The development of a Python library with geospatial data analysis tools is an essential step in making these methods more accessible to researchers and practitioners. The algorithm developed to automate the process successfully applied in eight South African provinces can be equally effective in other regions. The research highlights the potential of using smartphone GPS data to improve access to healthcare services, and it is crucial to note that this method may not fully account for factors such as transportation costs and road conditions that affect travel times. Nevertheless, this approach significantly expands our understanding of access to healthcare facilities. The research also addresses the potential biases inherent in using GPS data, such as non-representative sampling and data suppression. The potential of leveraging digital technology to improve access to healthcare services is vast, and it is essential to enhance the equity in health access, particularly in developing countries. The research demonstrates that strategy optimization techniques can significantly improve the reach of a service like Mother-Child HIV Care. SGLMs are a class of solvers that use implicit methods to solve initial value problems numerically by iteratively updating solution estimates until convergence is achieved. The method has been modified to work with non-uniform data grids, where solution estimates are updated at irregular intervals using existing data points, thereby increasing its flexibility. In this study, SGLMs were extended to accommodate non-uniform grids and tested on different initial value problems under various conditions. When implemented on non-uniform grids, SGLMs behave differently from their uniform grid counterparts due to non-uniform data-based solution updates. The study found that non-uniform SGLMs are particularly effective in problems where the error is predominantly due to data representation, such as in the case of step-size changes. When step-size changes occur infrequently, non-uniform SGLMs were found to successfully minimize solution errors in problems like the Schrödinger equation, where the error is primarily due to the solver. Conversely, step-size changes that occur frequently lead to significant solution errors and, in some cases, algorithmic failure. To address this issue, the non-uniform SGLMs were modified by incorporating additional data points through linear interpolation, thereby reducing solution errors and minimizing the occurrence of algorithmic failure. The study demonstrated that non-uniform SGLMs with interpolation can achieve accuracy comparable to machine precision in problems like the Schrödinger equation, where the error is predominantly due to the solver, and outperform uniform SGLMs in problems where the error is predominantly due to data representation. Furthermore, the non-uniform SGLMs with interpolation were found to successfully minimize solution errors in problems like the two-body problem, where the error is predominantly due to data representation, and even outperform uniform SGLMs when step-size changes occur infrequently. However, when step-size changes occur frequently, non-uniform SGLMs with interpolation still fail to match the performance of uniform SGLMs. To address this issue, the non-uniform SGLMs were modified by incorporating additional data points and using this information to make informed step-size changes, thereby minimizing the occurrence of algorithmic failure and increasing the effectiveness of non-uniform SGLMs. The study demonstrated that non-uniform SGLMs with interpolation and dynamic step-size control can achieve accuracy comparable to machine precision in problems like the two-body problem, and even outperform uniform SGLMs in such problems, and even successfully apply to problems where the solution components fall outside the range of IEEE floating-point numbers. This paper explores portfolio optimization in a market where wealth and the market index are linked by a non-linear factor. Investors are assumed to make decisions based on a financial function that takes into account both absolute and relative wealth. To address this complex problem, a unified solution is developed using a dynamic approach within the Levy-Alpha-Stieljes process framework, which encompasses both Gaussian and non-Gaussian environments. Furthermore, a numerical method based on polynomial approximation is proposed to support the proposed solution. The validity of the proposed solution is confirmed through numerical examples. Additionally, a classification method is used to determine the optimal investment strategy for different types of financial functions, including logarithmic, power, exponential, and Weibull utilities. For instance, the logarithmic utility requires complete positive wealth, while the power utility requires sufficient wealth. In contrast, both absolute and relative wealth are crucial for the exponential utility, while the Weibull utility relies on both, but with a higher dependence on relative wealth for smaller wealth levels. Overall, this research offers an extensive portfolio optimization solution within a non-Gaussian environment, leveraging a numerical method based on polynomial approximation. By incorporating relative wealth into the utility function, this work addresses a key real-world issue associated with portfolio optimization in a non-linear market. Nevertheless, the use of relative wealth still poses challenges, such as the problem of zero or negative wealth. Consequently, the proposed solution incorporates a numerical method based on polynomial approximation to mitigate these issues in a unified and accurate manner. The solution is shown to converge numerically to an existing solution in a Gaussian environment and is specifically simplified within a Gaussian environment. To illustrate the power and efficiency of the proposed method, a numerical simulation is performed for different parameter scenarios. For instance, the solution is shown to be effective in identifying optimal investment strategies in an exponential market when the utility function exhibits a power law. In another instance, the solution requires taking into account both absolute and relative wealth when the market is characterized by non-Gaussian and linear trends. In general, the solution offers an effective and accurate solution to portfolio optimization problems in different market environments, utility functions, and probability environments. In particular, the solution offers an easy-to-use and accurate method for power functions with a coefficient greater than one. In contrast, the solution offers a method that accounts for both absolute and relative wealth in non-Gaussian environments, but requires modification for power functions with a coefficient less than one. The analysis of quasiparticles in materials involves understanding how a mobile, interacting system behaves in the presence of fixed, scattering sites. To investigate this phenomenon, a fermion-boson model has been developed, incorporating the movement of both particles and their interaction rules. By examining the resulting collective excitations, the effects of different interaction parameters on the fermionic quasiparticles can be assessed. A scattering ab initio study of graphene and a subsystem of cuprates, involving a single layer of CuO, has revealed unique quasiparticle characteristics that are comparable across the two systems. However, the ferromagnetic ordering observed in the CuO layer results in quasiparticles that exhibit enhanced effective masses and a specific g-factor. Furthermore, the model's applicability is explored in quasiparticle spectra observation in the scanning tunnelling microscope. By quantitatively interpreting the tunnelling data, the density of states associated with fermionic quasiparticles can be quantified. Consequently, the effectiveness of a specific g- factor approximation in the CuO layer is established. By leveraging this information, the density of states associated with heavy quasiparticles can be calculated, resulting in a quasiparticle contribution to the zero-bias tunnelling peak of approximately 65%. Consequently, the relevance of light, mobile fermions in this phenomenon is confirmed. Therefore, the density of states associated with light, mobile fermions can be calculated by subtracting the quasiparticle contribution from the total quasiparticle density, yielding a quasiparticle density of approximately 35%. In the process, the concept of tunnelling into a state with a negative effective mass requires a reinterpretation due to the possibility of a positive effective mass in the relativistic limit. By considering this reevaluation, the graph theory analysis of the tunneling data can be performed, resulting in the assignment of a specific index to the fermionic quasiparticle in the CuO layer. Specifically, the quasiparticle density of states in the CuO layer has been identified as the 7th node in the graph. Obtaining accurate evaluations methods in NLP often relies on human annotations, but the variation in quality among these annotations poses a problem.  To address this issue, we propose a qualification pipeline that leverages various types of annotations.  By utilizing a combination of initial, intermediate, and final annotations in a pipeline, we ensure that only high-quality annotations are utilized for developing effective evaluations, much like how peer-review processes evaluate scientific studies.  We apply this pipeline to an automatic summarization dataset, cross-validate its effectiveness, and demonstrate that it enables development of reliable evaluations, ultimately leading to better performance.  Notably, the qualified labels obtained through this process can facilitate not only evaluations but also other applications such as data augmentation and active learning, resulting in substantial improvements.  By achieving labels of similar quality at a cost that is roughly 1/10th of the original, we showcase the value of our qualification pipeline.  Moreover, we highlight the significance of intermediate labels in this process and prove that utilizing various annotation types is advantageous.  Importantly, we establish that an efficient evaluation method depends on the specific task and represents a trade-off between various task-specific metrics - precision, recall, and F1-score.  The quality of intermediate labels, in particular, plays a crucial role in achieving optimal evaluation performance.  Consequently, using the qualification pipeline to enhance intermediate labels results in significant improvement of evaluation performance.  The new evaluation method we develop achieves better performance across three metrics - accuracy, ROUGE scores, and latency - in an automatic summarization challenge.  Specifically, our evaluation method outperches in terms of latency, requiring only 1 second to process a batch of 10 questions, and surpasses the best human performance in metrics such as answer accuracy and semantic accuracy.  Importantly, our evaluation method even outperches the performance of a trained human, indicating that current human evaluators in a leading dataset make about 20 mistakes per question, which is deemed suboptimal.  We hope that our qualification pipeline will be adopted in other NLP datasets to enhance both human and future machine-based evaluations.  The pipeline source code, datasets, and other relevant materials are available at https://github.com/guiguiguiguigui/Annotation_Quality_Evaluation.  Finally, our paper receives an award at the 2020 Conference, being nominated as one of the three outstanding papers out of 96.  The award presentation can be viewed at https://youtu.be/3tC3Q1. Random networks combining elements of both preferential attachment and independent uniform graph models have been created, resulting in hybrid networks with distinct degree distributions. Compared to purely preferential attachment networks, these hybrid networks have fewer high-degree connections to a smaller number of nodes and more high-degree connections to a greater number of nodes. As a result, hybrid networks more closely resemble real-world networks, which are characterized by a smaller number of highly connected nodes. We have investigated the properties of these hybrid random networks, specifically their in- and out-degree distributions, clustering coefficients, and the distribution of shortest paths length. We have also demonstrated that even with random hybrid networks, the separation between in- and out-degree distributions is more pronounced than in purely random or purely preferential attachment graphs. Furthermore, the size of this difference is heavily influenced by the parameter governing the preferential attachment mechanism and can be quantified using the inverse of the Laplacian's smallest eigenvalue. We have further explored the spectral properties of these hybrid networks and shown that changes in the preferential attachment parameter can be detected from changes in the spacing between consecutive eigenvalues in the graph's Laplacian matrix. We have presented numerical simulations illustrating these findings, which are verified for sufficiently large network sizes. We demonstrate that a good approximation of the in- and out-degree distributions can be achieved by considering only the first few eigenvalues of the graph's Laplacian matrix, which can be computed in polynomial time. We discuss the implications of these findings, which suggest that the spectral properties of these hybrid networks offer a robust indicator of the preferential attachment mechanism, and therefore can be used to infer the presence of this mechanism in real-world networks. Given the relatively simple structure of these hybrid networks, as well as their easy computability in large scales, we propose them as an excellent candidate for the design of asymmetric, artificial hyperbolic networks. Spartan enables a controlled exploration of the generative power of neural networks by introducing 'quasi-thermodynamic' behaviors during training. By balancing the exploration of the network's generative space with the need to pinpoint the optimal solution, Spartan offers an adaptable and efficient solution for identifying high-quality sparse sub-networks within large neural network architectures. Spartan's training process is characterized by an initial, highly exploratory phase where all parameters are active, followed by a later, more targeted phase where only relevant parameters are optimized. By employing a information-theoretic regularizer, Spartan can pinpoint the specific sub-network components required for optimal solution resolution. Our evaluation of Spartan on challenging image classification tasks reveals that it can efficiently discover sparse neural networks that match or surpass the performance of state-of-the-art models while also significantly reducing computational costs and memory requirements. For instance, Spartan can discover a 99.9% pruned ResNet-50 model while only utilizing 1/10 of the parameters and 1/5 of the computational resources required by the unpruned model while achieving comparable accuracy. Our results also demonstrate that Spartan's trained sub-networks can robustly generalize against unseen data, passing the robustness challenge established by Google AI Experiments. Furthermore, Spartan can be used in conjunction with other pruning algorithms to further enhance its performance. Our thorough evaluation of Spartan across multiple architectures and datasets enables us to provide direct answers to crucial questions regarding its adaptability in dealing with diverse tasks, datasets, and scales of input data. Although researchers have identified several types of test smells, their practical impact on software development remains unclear. Our investigation focuses on how professional developers perceive and address two common test smells, redundant test methods and overly broad test methods. We designed two surveys, one aimed at evaluating the severity of these test smells and their effects on maintainability, and another targeting practitioners to understand the frequency and causes of these test smells. The first survey involved 21 experts who shared similar opinions, suggesting these test smells are considered moderately severe. Additionally, they believe redundant test methods have a considerable impact on maintainability, whereas overly broad test methods have a minor one. Our second survey revealed that redundant test methods are seen more frequently than overly broad methods. Interestingly, developers link the occurrence of redundant test methods to less experienced teams, whereas overly broad test methods are seen as a result of poor testing practices. Notably, developers propose multiple approaches to address redundant test methods, including automated tools, but stress the need for manual intervention in the case of overly broad test methods. Our research highlights practical implications for practitioners and developers, suggesting the effectiveness of automated solutions for redundant test smells but stress the need for human judgment in the case of overly broad test methods. Furthermore, developers recommend the adoption of regular review processes and test process analysis to prevent the appearance of overly broad test methods. However, they propose the use of test process analysis only after successful implementation of test first strategies. Finally, our study suggests the effectiveness of static analysis tools in identifying redundant test methods but emphasizes the need for dynamic analysis to accurately classify overly broad test methods. The complete survey questionnaires are available on the Zenodo repository at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5100500. This research introduces a novel class of integro-differential processes called integro-differential sweeping processes, which combine elements of differential sweeping processes with integral constraints. These processes are defined by an evolution equation with an integrand that relies on the solution and an initial value, along with a set-valued mapping that determines the dynamic behavior of the solution. The paper demonstrates the existence and continuity of solutions with respect to initial values for these processes in Banach spaces without requiring smoothness. Additionally, it investigates the stability of solutions for systems of differential equations with impulsive effects and provides an example of an integro-differential sweeping process in a Banach space. The study ultimately highlights the potential applications of these processes to modeling dynamic systems with memory and impulsive behavior. Several fundamental theorems have been established, including those related to existence, uniqueness, and stability of solutions, as well as continuity and dependence. Impulse effects on the solution are exemplified through a case study of a physical system in a Banach space, described by an integro-differential differential equation with impulsive components. The research proves the existence and continuity of solutions for this particular system using a combination of set-valued homotopy results and Lyapunov-type methods. This investigation reveals new insights into the solution's behavior in impulsive integro-differential systems, shedding light on how impulses affect the solution through a two-dimensional example in $\mathbb{R}^2$. The study ultimately contributes to a deeper understanding of general integro-differential sweeping processes by deriving implications for differential and impulsive differential equations as special cases. The research concludes by providing concrete examples to illustrate the application of existence and stability theorems to real-world models, including a single pendulum system with impulsive effects and a pair of pendulums with pendulum-free motion. The solutions to these examples reveal the pendulums' behavior under impulsive effects at different time moments. The research concludes by outlining open questions and potential avenues for future investigation, including obtaining smooth dependence results, adapting the model to vector-valued mappings, and exploring novel applications. One such application lies in the dynamic modeling of seismic mounds with memory, involving an integro-differential differential equation describing the process of a solid being subjected to an impulse. The solution's behavior in this context reveals a decrease in the size of the seismic mound as the impulse decreases. The research concludes by highlighting the dynamic features of the growing and shrinking of seismic mounds with memory, illustrating the potential for future investigations into the modeling of these phenomena.

Our approach leverages the Hilbert-schmidt norm of tensor-structured matrices to derive an efficient, randomized t-SVD computation method. In contrast to prior methods, our algorithm accommodates any number of passes over the data tensor, achieves optimal sample complexity, and ensures precise computation of singular values and the singular vector subspace spanned by the data. Embedding graphs dynamically has emerged as a vital task for capturing both the node attributes and link connections of complex networks over time. Although existing techniques primarily focus on detecting community structures, the problem of encoding graphs dynamically remains underexplored. In this study, we present Diff2AE, a two-stage method for graph embedding that leverages an attentional approach to encode graph sequences. Diff2AE begins by generating node embeddings through attentional encoding of the initial graph, followed by a edge encoding process that combines current and previous time-step embeddings to generate edge embeddings. The method updates all node and edge embeddings at each time step. Our comparative evaluations on five real-world graphs demonstrate that Diff2AE outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, with notable gains of up to $7\%$ in ISO NMI metric, while also producing comparable results to the best techniques in terms of ISO NMI metrics for the initial snapshots of the graphs, slightly improving upon them in some cases. Furthermore, Diff2AE exhibits superior robustness to temporal shifts compared to other techniques, indicating its value in real-world applications that involve graph dynamic analysis. The code for Diff2AE has been made publicly available on GitHub at the specified URL. Our experimental findings also highlight potential issues of overfitting for graph dynamic embedding methods, which may lead to inaccurate predictions when graph structure changes over time. It has been observed that all methods we compared exhibit overfitting and node embedding drift over time, which could be alleviated with edge embedding updates based on current graph structure, as Diff2AE does. Moreover, our analysis reveals that the learned node embeddings in Diff2AE are highly correlated with community labels, while those of other methods do not show such correlation. These findings suggest the potential of the underlying technique in Diff2AE for discovering node representations that are temporally invariant. To achieve this, we identified a new approach called Temporal Invariance Criterion (TIC) that assembles sequences of graph embeddings from different methods and evaluates their temporal invariance using ISO NMI metric. Our analysis using TIC showed that Diff2AE has better temporal invariance compared to other methods, which again underscores the potential of the underlying technique in Diff2AE for discovering node representations that are temporally invariant. Researchers at the BBN EPIC system discovered a previously unknown low-energy resonance in $^7$H, which likely has a very narrow structure. This finding might influence the understanding of how lightest neutrinos interact at very low energy levels. Given its energy range, it's possible that this resonance could have significant implications for how neutrinos of minimal mass interact and contribute to baryon asymmetry in the universe, particularly through a process known as the neutrinoless process of lepton number violation. To further understand the characteristics of this resonance, which was identified for the first time, it's necessary to analyze $^7$H ground state photodisintegration. A new theoretical model was developed specifically for this purpose, one which treats the $^7$H ground state as composed of three-body clusters, and employs the hyperspherical harmonic method. Using this model, which was validated by comparing it to existing data, researchers were able to calculate and provide new cross-section data for the photodisintegration process that removes protons from $^7$H in two stages. They also extracted rates for protons emitted from $^7$H in two stages. These calculations matched recent experimental measurements by a team at the MAMI accelerator facility in Germany. Importantly, they revealed that a narrow low-energy resonance at approximately 0.5 MeV (denoted as $^7$H$_{10}$) could significantly influence the cross-section data and proton emission rates observed at this specific energy level. This resonance, which has a very narrow structure, was not predicted by existing theoretical models based on cluster effective field theories. Consequently, there are two possible explanations for its origin: the resonance could be a $^6$H nucleus attached to a neutron or, alternatively, an $\alpha$ particle bonded to a deuteron. Further research is necessary to distinguish between these two potential explanations for this narrow low-energy resonance. Furthermore, it is also necessary to analyze whether a narrow low-energy resonance at approximately 0.5 MeV could significantly influence existing data related to big-bang nucleosynthesis in $^7$Li production, and whether a more precise calculation of this cross-section and proton emission rates is required to determine $^7$H($\gamma$,n)$ at higher energies above 1 MeV.

Conventional methods typically employ a single loss function for feature learning, such as the weakly-supervised contrastive loss. However, this approach often leads to overlapping feature points on the same image, hindering the formation of distinct discriminative embedding spaces. To address this issue, we introduce the Deep Class-wise Discrepancy Loss (DCDL), a proposed method that can break down class-wise similarities and enhance the separation of features in the embedding space during backpropagation. As more agents begin to learn in real-world settings, the need is growing for ways to effectively communicate the expectations that govern their behavior. A promising approach to this challenge involves utilizing the agents' internally learned constraints to facilitate better understanding and more informed decision-making. This paper explores the idea of utilizing these learned constraints as a form of abstract specification. We develop a principled framework for identifying these constraints and introduce a formal representation, called learned congruence, which captures typical pattern occurrences. This representation is then applied to specify and verify agent behavior across various scenarios. Moreover, we demonstrate that the expectations defined by learned congruences can be aligned with the agents' training objectives, allowing us to reflect these expectations back into the agents through updated reward signals. This reward updating process enables agents to relearn constraints that are more in line with the desired specifications. We evaluate our approach by examining its applicability to constraint-abiding agents and markov decision processes. The results show that the reward updating process can lead to significant improvements in constraint alignment while only requiring minimal additional training for the agents. This is in addition to other benefits, including the discovery of untrained safety constraints and the identification of agent limitations. Consequently, the techniques presented in this study offer practitioners valuable tools for specifying, verifying, and fine-tuning agent behavior. They also facilitate a deeper understanding of the role of constraints in learned behavior. These techniques, although presented in the context of learned constraints, can theoretically be applied to other forms of abstract specifications as well. All the source code and models used in this study are publicly available at https://github.com/tefra98/learned-constraints. Initial observations of zero-bias anomalies in scanning tunneling spectroscopy have been attributed to two distinct phenomena: zero-energy peaks resulting from Majorana modes and non-Majorana caused zero-energy peaks. Recent comparisons of experimental data to calculated transport characteristics using the non-Majorana model have led some researchers to conclude that the real physical properties of zero-energy peaks at zero temperature. Employing the non-Majorana model, we investigate how the zero-energy peaks evolve under the influence of finite temperatures. Similar to majorana modes, zero-energy peaks exhibit a temperature-dependent shift. Unlike majorana modes, however, this shift remains proportional to temperature, rendering measurements impossible without accounting for temperature. We provide temperature-based estimates for measuring Majorana modes based on their temperature-dependent shift in comparison to majorana modes. We also calculate the average conductance along with fluctuating values within a temperature range to help distinguish between majorana and non-Majorana modes based on their temperature-dependent characteristics. Furthermore, we show that the suppression of zero-energy peaks results from a shift in Fermi energy towards a localised subband rather than a shift resulting from a finite temperature Bose condensate. This distinction is analogous to a debate on whether zero-energy peaks are caused by zero or finite temperature effects. Similarly, we investigate the origin of zero-energy peaks by deriving an analytical expression for the local density of states resulting from a finite temperature Bose condensate and establish that the local density of states does not exhibit a zero-energy peak but instead a continuous increase towards the upper bound of a finite energy range. We conclude that the observed suppression of zero-energy peaks could be caused by a shift resulting from a finite temperature Bose condensate rather than a zero-energy peak resulting from a finite temperature Bose condensate, rendering the zero-energy anomaly a phenomenon inconsistent with a zero-energy peak resulting solely from a finite temperature Bose condensate. This study also provides a finite-temperature analogy to an analytical expression for zero-energy peaks derived in a zero-temperature environment, showing that distinct properties exist between zero and finite temperatures. However, these effects often yield ambiguous measurements due to possible compensations between valley and orbital Hall conductivity.  But the orbital Hall effect stands out as a more reliable measure of the valley index, enabling direct contact with the valley degree of freedom.  In this work, we take advantage of the orbital Hall effect to investigate the valley index in GaAs/AlGaAs quantum wells through the application of a transverse electric field.  By examining various quantum states in these quantum wells, we verify that the valley index is successfully identified for a range of these states.  But in contrast, attempts to access the valley index in a ground state of a different spin-polarization level are hindered by compensating contributions from orbital Hall conductivity.  Our investigation into this phenomenon suggests that the valley index is successfully coupled with the orbital Hall effect, enabling reliable measurements of valley indices even in systems with multiple energy levels.  Importantly, our analysis reveals that existing imbalances in effective masses do not adequately account for compensating orbital Hall conductivity in this system, indicating that a deeper microscopic analysis is required to address this phenomenon. The comparison also reveals a change in sign of valley Hall conductivity in a state of negative effective mass, correlating with predictions of a left-handed valley Hall effect in this system.
