While traditional tools for class hierarchy visualization lack clear indicators of hierarchical depth, our OntoPlot account is designed to address this limitation and enhance visual understanding. By incorporating new visual elements and an interactive framework, OntoPlot helps users to more easily navigate and comprehend ontology structures. Its enhanced visual features, such as bubble sizes and colors, accurately convey the depth of hierarchical relationships, rather than just focusing on class names and irrevocable hierarchies. This interactive capability allows users to instantly respond to these visual cues, gaining valuable insights into the composition of the ontology. Moreover, OntoPlot facilitates the discovery of incomplete or unsatisfactory visualizations, allowing users to identify and rectify ambiguities in the ontology. As a result, OntoPlot proves to be an indispensable tool for daily ontology visualization needs. Furthermore, a comparative analysis with Systematin's OntoPlot is presented, highlighting its limitations in visualizing shallow and complex hierarchies. This comparison serves as a recommendation for Systematin's OntoPlot to be utilized primarily for large and deeply structured ontologies, whereas OntoPlot should be preferred when visualizing more complex or extensive ontologies. The final implementation of OntoPlot is made available on GitHub, accompanied by a demonstration of its interactive functionality. Additionally, a step-by-step tutorial on OntoPlot's development is provided. The potential future directions for OntoPlot's development are also explored, such as its future integration with Google Scholar to visualize authorship relationships within the ontology community. Furthermore, a potential extension to visualize the geographical distribution of authors is discussed, delving into the potential drawbacks and challenges of such a visualization method. By integrating these additional features, OntoPlot can be further optimized to serve as an indispensable tool for discovering, evaluating, and sustaining (DES) ontology communities. Ultimately, a vision for a fully automated and sustainable OntoPlot development framework is presented, paving the way for the next chapter in OntoPlot's development. This vision is made possible by automating the process of OntoPlot's design, paving the way for the creation of a design template similar to the ones used by Google Web Designer and Adobe XD. Consequently, a sustainable development model is proposed, delving into the potential issues and challenges of such a template-based design framework. Prior work on these models often specialized or hardened them for specific data types, and currently there's a knowledge gap on their applications to diverse sensory data. To bridge this gap, we demonstrate the potential of these models in unstructured sensory data from a large movie dataset, encompassing optical flows, audios, and natural language subtitles. We showcase their capabilities in novel generative applications, including video audio and text synthesis, and text-to-video and audio generation. This work aims to empower the development of future generative models that learn from unstructured sensory data. The code and dataset can be found at https://github.com/quantifiedself-upv/MovieQA-sensory-generative-models. E.R. Vali is also the corresponding author.

Recent research suggests that pre-trained transformer models can achieve high performance in various tasks by fine-tuning.  Despite ongoing discussions about the efficiency of these models, they have significant drawbacks, such as needing massive computing resources and large datasets to function optimally after fine-tuning.  To change this, we propose a novel pre-trained transformer-based approach for task-agnostic data augmentation, aiming to produce datasets suitable for downstream tasks that are more resource-efficient.  This method incorporates a data augmentation module into the pre-training stage, allowing for the creation of enhanced datasets in later stages.  We tested and analyzed this approach with WMT16 English data and several other datasets in task-agnostic data augmentation and learned to generate high-quality text that is comparable to human standards.  Furthermore, we demonstrated that fine-tuning smaller, more nuanced models can achieve performance that is on par with larger, more resource-intensive models in multiple downstream tasks, including essay scoring and question answering.  To facilitate future research, we are releasing our approach and associated resources publicly for the research community. A common issue in learning to tackle the false positive problem arises due to data imbalance. To address this, our approach converges the problem to a box re-ranking task. This allows the model to learn effective false positive suppression, even in the absence of labeled data, through a user-specified query. We develop two solutions to achieve this: first, we map the initial problem into a re-ranking one with a relevant loss function, using the Karlin-Szegoe distance. Secondly, we propose a loss function optimized for re-ranking, based on the Generalized Jaccard Index. We evaluate these methods on three high-energy physics datasets, revealing that the approach using the Karlin-Szegoe distance outperforms the one based on the Generalized Jaccard Index and existing supervised methods. Moreover, we compare the results to a conventional re-ranking method, demonstrating their relative effectiveness. This study highlights the feasibility of unsupervised false positive suppression, even with minimal human intervention. We provide a publicly accessible framework to tackle this problem. This framework is hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/antoinelemieux/FPUnsupervised. We also contribute to Energy Physics a new method for accurate jet sub-structure analysis, specifically task-driven unsupervised rejection of prominent camera artifacts. This technique leverages the defined query and utilizes the Karlin-Szegoe distance. It utilizes the widely used GlowNN neural network to achieve the rejection, and we make this network available through the framework as well. Additionally, we introduce Energy Physics with a new method for accurate jet sub-structure analysis, specifically task-driven unsupervised rejection of prominent camera artifacts. This technique leverages the defined query and utilizes the Karlin-Szegoe distance, combined with the GlowNN neural network, made available through the framework. Moreover, we provide the framework with an implementation of the GlowNN neural network, widely used for glowstick-based imaging, now repurposed for the rejection of prominent camera artifacts. We also extend the GlowNN neural network with a binary splitter, allowing it to achieve superior binary classification performance. Current top-performing NMT models often rely on syntax-aware attention models that consider sentence syntax in the source language to guide the attention mechanism. We have developed novel regularized versions of several popular machine learning algorithms, incorporating two innovative techniques: transmutations and mixed mutations. Unlike traditional label transformations like cosine similarity and softmax that maintain the original class order, transmutations map one class to multiple others, while mixed mutations combine the strengths of label embeddings and cosine similarity. Our proposed algorithms, including a regularized k-nearest neighbor, a regularized support vector machine, and a regularized convolutional neural network, demonstrate the potential of these new techniques, especially for imbalanced datasets. Through experimentation with well-known datasets, we have successfully improved the accuracy and F1 score in margin-based and deep learning classifiers, respectively. Furthermore, we have observed a positive impact on accuracy and reduced variance in classifier training. These new techniques have been released as an open-source library called MuMu at https://mu-mu.github.io.

A novel, augmented-label coupling method for training models is introduced and proven effective in supervised models for visual tasks. Specifically, we propose using image augmentations to expand limited labeled data for model training, ultimately reducing the necessity for extensive annotated images. In the context of detecting pneumonia using chest X-rays, our method demonstrates the capability to diminish the needed annotated samples by half while maintaining detection accuracy comparable to full annotation. The utility of this technique is also demonstrated in other visual tasks, such as solving the scope segmentation problem with dextrous hand instrument images where our model achieves the best results with annotated samples reduced by 85%. Furthermore, we provide an end-to-end differentiable solution for coupling that does not necessitate additional training for inverse transformations. This approach improves the efficiency of data augmentation in the inference process. In summary, we present a versatile, adaptive data augmentation strategy that can be seamlessly integrated with supervised models for various visual tasks. However, existing frameworks for coherent and complete causation lack the structural components necessary for accurate application. To address this limitation, we developed a novel representation of contrastive causation grounded in utility theory, thereby integrating concepts of harm and utility into a unified framework for assessing causes and effects. This formulation builds on the principles of quantified consequence assessment, utilizing propositional formulas to evaluate the likelihood and utility of various actions and their consequences. By combining these principles with a specific value structure, we can effectively identify the most effective measures to prevent or mitigate adverse effects, thereby preserving desirable outcomes and maximizing overall utility. Our new concept of contrastive causality extends existing ideas on causation by enabling precise evaluation of consequences, effects, and interactions among multiple causes. Moreover, we introduced novel logical operators that facilitate easy application of this concept to diverse scenarios, thereby providing a comprehensive toolkit for maximizing utility and minimizing harm. This new representation of contrastive causation enables a deeper understanding of interaction between utility and harm, as demonstrated in our analysis of utility and harm in decision-making processes. To facilitate practical use of this concept, we developed a natural deduction system that provides sound and complete derivations for utility and harm assessment, as well as an algorithm for automated calculation of these values. By extending the principles of quantified consequence assessment and utility theory, we can ensure the practical applicability of this concept to diverse domains. Full technical specifications of our approach are provided within the article. As illustrated in our evaluation, the practical understanding of utility and harm developed here has significant implications for their assessment in decision-making processes. To further illustrate the practical relevance of our formal framework, we analyzed the complex scenario of human decision-making during the Syrian Civil War and demonstrated how our concept of contrastive causation can effectively identify the most relevant factors contributing to that conflict. Similar applications of this concept to other domains are also feasible. The integration of deep learning in wildlife conservation is a rapidly evolving field that holds significant potential for advancing wildlife monitoring, research, and conservation. However, most current wildlife applications of deep learning are restricted to high-quality images, neglecting the vast, often unexplored wildlife-related image resources awaiting exploration. Moreover, the advancement of deep learning in wildlife conservation is often hindered by practical limitations, such as access to computing resources and image processing capabilities. This study presents an easy-to-implement, computationally efficient deep learning model for classifying images, requiring minimal computational power and memory. The model is based on residual neural networks and incorporates a hierarchical architecture with a progressive learning structure, enabling the detection of rare classes. By integrating the efficient network with data augmentation techniques, the study demonstrates the feasibility of developing a deep learning model suitable for analysis of large-scale image datasets on low-resource hardware, such as laptops or Android tablets. This would enable researchers to easily analyze and explore unexplored image resources, including those from video content, such as TV channels and social media platforms, to support wildlife conservation efforts. The proposed model achieved a high accuracy of 91.2% on a dataset of bird images from African TV channels and a medium computational cost of 0.53 seconds per frame, compatible with real-time processing on low-resource hardware. The model's source code is publicly available on the GitHub platform. The study suggests that mass adoption of deep learning in wildlife conservation efforts at the grassroots level, particularly on mobile devices, could greatly contribute to the development of a data-driven decision-making approach for effective conservation management. This would facilitate data integration from multiple sources, including citizen science, to support large-scale data-intensive conservation applications. Ultimately, this could assist conservation biologists and managers in making informed decisions about species classification, particularly in complex scenarios involving the estimation of CS/CS+ noise ratios in datasets, to support species detection and real-time wildlife monitoring. Such conservation tools, tailored to the capabilities of low-resource hardware, have the potential to make a significant positive impact on the effective conservation management of individual species, particularly in developing countries. The widespread availability of deep learning models on open-source platforms, such as GitHub, indicates the significant success of conservation-driven initiatives to make these models accessible to end-users, particularly in countries with limited research capabilities. At the practical level, this study's findings suggest the feasibility of processing large-scale datasets on low-resource hardware, enabling researchers to easily analyze unexplored image resources, such as video content, to support effective wildlife conservation efforts. These models are part of a broader class of generalized heat conduction equations, which have been extensively reviewed in the literature. While the models are mathematically consistent, their derivation is often problematic due to the influence of non-physical artifacts. In contrast, our approach derives a complete heat conduction equation with a memory component using a constitutive relation, thus eliminating unnecessary model assumptions. This method allows the derivation of models that mimic the distributed-order heat conduction equation and other non-traditional models. Furthermore, we re-examine the fundamental principles of heat conduction and establish a connection between the traditional Fourier law and constitutive relations with memory. This analysis reveals that the classical heat conduction equation is a limiting case of the first law of thermodynamics, which governs energy changes in systems over time. In addition, we develop a second-law-based analysis for the distributed-order heat conduction equation and establish its validity under conditions of thermal balance. Furthermore, we illustrate the applicability of these models using an example from the literature. To create accurate models for guiding renewable energy curtailment and energy investment, accurate energy forecasts are essential. Current advanced neural network forecasts, particularly for short-term energy forecasting, exhibit high accuracy but often fail to learn from previous predictions. In contrast, traditional forecasts like AR and ARMA, which are based on past data, can be overlooked in recent deep learning models. To address this limitation and unlock the full potential of traditional forecasting techniques, we propose a novel method called ARIF, which fuses peak forecasts with conventional forecasts through an iterative fusion approach. By leveraging this approach, ARIF has outperformed state-of-the-art models like ProPhesee and Temporal Neural Network in 1-3 hours ahead real-time energy forecasting, offering improved accuracy and efficiency. Our research also demonstrates that integrating peak and conventional forecasting can augment non-sequential models and boost their performance when applied sequentially. We conduct an in-depth analysis and visualization of ARIF's internal representation to provide insight into its internal mechanisms. Furthermore, we evaluate ARIF's robustness under data anomalies and forecasting challenges, revealing its capacity to adapt and remain effective. Overall, our research introduces ARIF as a versatile and efficient approach for short-term energy forecasting across various scenarios and data conditions. We anticipate that ARIF can serve as a baseline for future research in short-term energy forecasting. Our code and model will be publicly available for reproduction and verification. With further refinement, ARIF has the potential to enhance peak demand forecasting during critical hours, contributing significantly to the development of neural network-based energy models for data-driven operations and investment. Nevertheless, in scenarios requiring high accuracy and data consistency, ARIF's performance may be compromised by data anomalies and changes, revealing areas for potential enhancement. To address this limitation, we propose the application of anomaly detection and representation learning to uncover underlying patterns and improve ARIF's robustness in the future. Lastly, we reveal ARIF's potential for widespread use in energy forecasting, but also highlight its shortcomings and room for future research and innovation. The rise of machine learning has significantly impacted data-driven decision-making in various fields, enabling the identification of intricate patterns in datasets and predicting complex outcomes. Although machine learning techniques excel without additional guidance, incorporating relevant knowledge can enhance their performance, accuracy, and overall dependability. In this research, an extensive review of known and novel methodologies in scalable incremental learning is conducted, and the notion that knowledge augmentation is a promising approach to augment machine learning systems is presented. To this end, a new framework, known as Knowledge-Augmented Incremental Learning (KA-IL), is proposed, which integrates static and dynamic knowledge into incremental learning models for practical use in various applications. Furthermore, a comprehensive experimental evaluation is carried out on open-source incremental learning datasets to validate the proposed KA-IL framework, and three promising techniques for incorporating knowledge into incremental learning models are recommended for further development. Finally, potential future research avenues are suggested, including the exploration of semi-supervised and transductive settings, and the development of a unified KA-IL framework. In total, eight datasets and eight knowledge augmentation techniques for incremental learning are discussed. The datasets examined include charades-seg, uaw-celeb, mskd, msu-mobility, msu-family, uaw-far, msu-coffee, msu-garment, uce-hair, uce-eyes, uce-hands, uce-head, and uce-face. The knowledge augmentation techniques encompassed by this research include one-shot rotation, point-cloud registration, generative adversarial networks, metric learning, memory-augmented neural networks, online shrinkage, tensor decomposition, and feature selection. This multi-task learning framework combines two key tasks: a lesion detection system and a lesion type classification system, with each sharing a common feature map. To enhance performance, an algorithm using an augmented dataset generated from the original training data is also implemented. This augmented data framework exploits patterns in the training images to inform the placement of lesions during augmentation, thereby improving performance on unseen images. Following training, a latent feature vector is obtained for each image, allowing for the generation of a compact, data-driven model that can pinpoint lesions on unseen images. This approach was evaluated using 1,000 images from the RSNA Pneumonia Detection Challenge, yielding AUC values of 0.942, 0.933, and 0.932 for lesion detection, solid lesion detection, and lung lesion detection tasks, respectively. A new method for constructing costs in stereo matching involves analyzing occluded areas by assuming occlusions as part of the optimization process. This approach transposes costs, turning occluded pixels into unoccluded ones, and adapts occlusion masks on a per-disparity basis. Using a convolutional neural network, we leverage spatial coherence to further refine occlusion, and combine it with other costs through a convolutional operator. To enable effective optimization, we employ a mix-of-experts architecture that can adapt to the level of occlusion, and demonstrate significant reductions in disparities and occlusion errors by incorporating the proposed costs into existing frameworks. Notably, our constructor and adapter demonstrate comparable performance to a state-of-the-art unsupervised approach when assessed using the KITTI odometry evaluation metric. Most devices automatically connect to the nearest access point, but this can result in over-loaded access points which negatively impact devices' speeds and response times.  In an attempt to resolve this issue, we suggest a method where devices can determine the load on each access point before choosing which one to connect to.  This method allows devices to associate with the access point that offers the best connection and least amount of traffic. We also found that including load information in the association process is beneficial, even for smaller networks that are not affected by congestion issues.  To enable this method, our access point reports its load to a central server which then shares this information with devices on the network.
